title: Scam Defense Dashboard Twilio telephony ingress restoration, E.164 normalization & UI decluttering
snippet: Scam Defense Dashboard Twilio telephony ingress restoration, E.164 normalization & UI decluttering: With assistance from Antigravity AI, diagnosed and resolved an outbound telephony outage where calls stalled at “Queued / Connecting” with c...
content: Scam Defense Dashboard Twilio telephony ingress restoration, E.164 normalization & UI decluttering: With assistance from Antigravity AI, diagnosed and resolved an outbound telephony outage where calls stalled at “Queued / Connecting” with continuous ringback tones. Identified that while the private operator dashboard (port 8787) is secured within the Tailnet (port 10000), Twilio's cloud voice servers require public HTTPS/WSS ingress to deliver signed TwiML call instructions ( /twilio/voice/outbound ) and the bidirectional media stream ( /twilio/media ). Restored dedicated Tailscale Funnel ingress on port 443 pointing strictly to the signed Twilio webhook port 8788 ( tailscale funnel --bg --https=443 http://127.0.0.1:8788 ), ensuring the operator dashboard remains isolated from the public internet. Engineered a robust Unicode-aware phone number normalizer ( normalizePhoneNumber ) across the server and client that strips non-breaking spaces ( \u00A0 ), en-dashes ( – ), em-dashes, and hidden formatting characters to eliminate recurring “E.164 number required” validation rejections when pasting numbers from notes or contacts. Streamlined the case confirmation interface by removing the redundant 12-key on-screen dialpad to optimize screen space across desktop, tablet, and mobile browsers while preserving the in-call DTMF menu keypad.

Diagnosed that the startup script ( launch-dashboard.command ) previously configured Tailscale Funnel on port 443 ( tailscale funnel --bg --https=443 http://127.0.0.1:8788 ), which published a public internet endpoint ( https://the-macsimal-computing-experience.taile72a68.ts.net/ ) and displayed a public URL accessible to anyone on the open web whenever the application booted up. Decommissioned the public Funnel route entirely, purged the Funnel initialization routine from the launcher, and verified that only private Tailscale Serve remains active on port 10000 ( tailscale serve --bg --https=10000 http://127.0.0.1:8787 ) for secure, authenticated access exclusively from authorized devices inside the private tailnet. Hardened session cleanup in both launch-dashboard.command and the backup STOP-DASHBOARD.command to guarantee persistent Funnel teardown ( tailscale funnel --https=443 off ), updated project handoff documentation, and validated that zero internet links or public ingress routes are exposed upon bootup.

title: Alpine NUC Samba exFAT optimization & Windows SMB resource exhaustion triage
snippet: Alpine NUC Samba exFAT optimization & Windows SMB resource exhaustion triage: With assistance from Antigravity CLI, diagnosed and resolved Windows Explorer error 0x800705AA ( “Insufficient system resources exist to complete the requested se...
content: Alpine NUC Samba exFAT optimization & Windows SMB resource exhaustion triage: With assistance from Antigravity CLI, diagnosed and resolved Windows Explorer error 0x800705AA ( “Insufficient system resources exist to complete the requested service” ) and execution access failures ( “Windows cannot access” ) when accessing the shared exFAT USB storage drive ONEFIVE over Tailscale SMB ( B:\ ). Traced the execution failure to exFAT’s non-executable mount mask ( 0664 / fmask=0113 ) combined with missing Samba execute override policies; added acl allow execute always = yes to /etc/samba/smb.conf so Windows clients can execute scripts and binaries without failing Linux POSIX execute bit checks. Traced resource exhaustion during nested directory copying to Samba’s default attempts to store Windows DOS attributes and NTFS alternate streams in extended attributes ( xattr ), which the Linux kernel exFAT driver does not support, alongside leases database contention ( leases_db ndr_push character conversion error ); relocated smb2 leases = no to the [global] configuration block and disabled unsupported extended attributes ( ea support = no , store dos attributes = no ). Reloaded OpenRC service samba , validated nested directory copying and deletion over SMB, and repointed the desktop Minecraft server shortcut directly to the local execution target ( C:\Users\smbuser\MinecraftServer\start.bat ), safely removing the redundant network .bat file on the NUC share.

content: Linux Mint x11vnc TigerVNC handshake drop triage & passwordless Tailscale access: With assistance from Antigravity CLI, diagnosed and resolved an immediate connection drop issue where TigerVNC client windows abruptly terminated upon connecting to the persistent x11vnc remote desktop endpoints (port 5901 / display :1 at 1280x720, and port 5902 / display :2 at 1600x1264) on the Linux Mint HP laptop ( 100.110.13.11 ) following a kernel upgrade and system reboot. content: With assistance from Antigravity CLI, diagnosed and resolved an aggressive window focus stealing loop on the Debian Mac where Trayscale's GUI repeatedly forced itself open and captured keyboard input while typing. Investigation revealed an active race condition between XFCE session autostart ( ~/.config/autostart/trayscale.desktop ) and a user systemd service ( trayscale.service ) configured with Restart=always and RestartSec=5 . Because Trayscale operates as a single-instance GTK/GApplication app over D-Bus, every invocation of flatpak run dev.deedles.Trayscale --hide-window while the tray instance was already active sent an activation signal to the running process—causing it to unhide and focus its main window—before exiting immediately ( status=0 ). Systemd interpreted the clean exit as a process termination, waiting 5 seconds and triggering the launcher again in an infinite loop (exceeding 2,224 recorded restarts). Permanently stopped and disabled the redundant systemd unit, cleared failed restart states, and closed the lingering window, allowing Trayscale to run quietly and persistently in the XFCE system tray via standard desktop autostart.

content: With assistance from Antigravity CLI, diagnosed a remote desktop freeze and x11vnc connection timeout on the Debian Mac ( 100.117.166.66 ) following an intensive concurrent local image generation batch. Audited kernel event rings ( dmesg ) and system journal telemetry to isolate an acute out-of-memory condition where a Python generation process ballooned to ~99 GB virtual memory and 6.2 GB RSS, spiking system load to 69.21 and thrashing over 3.2 GB of swap until the Linux kernel OOM-killer intervened ( killed process 786272 (python) ). The resulting I/O starvation triggered a systemd-journald watchdog abort and dropped active RFB socket traffic ( Connection reset by peer ), severing the remote session. Further diagnosed LAN reconnection timeouts by inspecting the x11vnc systemd services ( x11vnc-1280x720.service and x11vnc-1600x1264.service ), uncovering that both instances are explicitly bound to the Tailscale IPv4 address ( -listen "100.117.166.66" ) rather than 0.0.0.0 , and that iptables drops incoming Tailscale subnet traffic arriving over physical LAN interfaces ( -A ts-input -s 100.64.0.0/10 ! -i tailscale0 -j DROP ). Confirmed display :0 and Tailscale daemon health fully recovered post-OOM, and verified RFB socket handshake responses on ports 5900 and 5901 over the Tailscale VPN adapter.

snippet: Slax Linux USB bare-metal UEFI & Legacy BIOS dual-mode bootloader repair, crash artifact purge & Windows XP SMB1 sync hardening: With assistance from Antigravity CLI, diagnosed and resolved bare-metal boot failures on the custom Debian 12 (...
content: Slax Linux USB bare-metal UEFI & Legacy BIOS dual-mode bootloader repair, crash artifact purge & Windows XP SMB1 sync hardening: With assistance from Antigravity CLI, diagnosed and resolved bare-metal boot failures on the custom Debian 12 (Bookworm) Slax persistence USB drive ( V:\ , SLAX_DEBIAN , 57.3 GB SanDisk 3.2 Gen 1) following prolonged session writes. For UEFI boot mode, diagnosed that \EFI\Boot\syslinux.cfg 's INCLUDE /slax/boot/syslinux.cfg directive forced the 64-bit UEFI binary ( bootx64.efi / syslinux.efi ) to execute an ELF 32-bit BIOS COM32 module ( /slax/boot/vesamenu.c32 ), triggering an immediate freeze at the EFI handover prompt; authored an isolated, self-contained UEFI configuration loading native 64-bit vesamenu.c32 directly from \EFI\Boot\ with an automated menu.c32 text fallback for graphics-sensitive GOP firmware. For Legacy BIOS boot mode, resolved the Syslinux 6.03 Failed to load ldlinux.c32 abort by copying missing runtime COM32 libraries ( ldlinux.c32 , libcom32.c32 , libutil.c32 , vesamenu.c32 ) into the drive root alongside ldlinux.sys . Additionally, scanned the FAT32 filesystem (0 bad sectors) and purged a 2.13 GB orphaned crash artifact ( FOUND.000\FILE0000.CHK ), expanding available volume space to 35.33 GB. Successfully booted the repaired drive bare-metal on the Dell Inspiron 3668 desktop, verifying dynamic session 1 loop mounting ( /memory/changes , 48 GB virtual capacity via dynfilefs ), automated XFCE desktop launch, Tailscale mesh node connectivity ( slax-desktop , 100.121.51.123 / 192.168.0.182 ), and dual background compute execution across Folding@home (PID 4302, FahCore_a8 ) and XMRig (PID 4258). Concurrently, overhauled the Windows XP legacy Wi-Fi sync pipeline ( sync_movies.bat and sync_all.bat ) on shared storage: eliminated the /C flag that masked network drops and falsely claimed completion, introduced direct UNC fallback ( \\192.168.0.205\G\09. Movies ) to bypass disconnected Y: drive mapping freezes on XP, and deployed automated SMB1 credential re-authentication ( smbuser:7131 ) on connection drops.

content: Circuit Playground Bluefruit Duino-Coin miner persistent LED blackout & uninterrupted USB mining: With assistance from Antigravity CLI, resolved an issue on the Adafruit Circuit Playground Bluefruit nRF52840 microcontroller (mounted over USB as drive E: with console serial on COM5 ) where the onboard 10-NeoPixel ring produced excessive brightness during Duino-Coin (DUCO) mining—flashing vibrant blue during SHA-1 job hashing, green upon accepted share discovery, orange during idle buffer polling, and red on errors. Enforced persistent zero-light operation across reboots and USB power cycles while preserving continuous, uninterrupted mining for Duino-Coin worker CircuitPlayground under account avanek737383 . Updated CircuitPython (10.2.1) firmware script E:\code.py and synchronized local workstation repository C:\Users\Owner\Duino-Circuit\code.py , enforcing zero brightness ( cp.pixels.brightness = 0 ), clearing the pixel ring ( cp.pixels.fill((0, 0, 0)) ), disabling the CircuitPython supervisor status pixel ( supervisor.runtime.rgb_status_brightness = 0 ), and forcing the red status LED off ( cp.red_led = False ). Stripped out runtime NeoPixel show operations during the mining loop, eliminating SPI bus timing overhead to increase hashing throughput (~2,851 H/s) and reduce thermal dissipation. Verified seamless runtime reload over USB CDC without disrupting the active Windows PowerShell serial orchestrator ( Start-Miner.ps1 ), confirming persistent dark operation and live accepted share progression against the Duino-Coin pool.

Created a custom udev hardware rule ( /etc/udev/rules.d/90-smc-kbd-backlight.rules ) matching the leds subsystem to enforce ATTR{brightness}="0" upon hardware module detection, deployed an early boot systemd oneshot unit ( /etc/systemd/system/keyboard-backlight-off.service ) ordered after systemd-backlight , and installed an executable systemd-sleep hook ( /usr/lib/systemd/system-sleep/keyboard-backlight-off.sh ) to reassert zero brightness immediately upon waking from ACPI suspend or hibernation. Validated complete zero-power persistence across an end-to-end cold reboot.

content: Follow-up / verification: With assistance from Antigravity CLI, recovered and verified the custom Slax Linux persistent installation on USB drive ( V:\ , SLAX_DEBIAN ) following an emergency forced power-down. Diagnosed that the sudden power loss left the host FAT32 filesystem flagged dirty ( Volume - V: is Dirty ) and caused incomplete metadata writes inside the backing 48 GB Dynfilefs sparse multi-slice container ( /slax/changes/1/changes.dat.* ). Reconciled the host partition using Windows chkdsk V: /f , clearing the dirty bit ( Volume - V: is NOT Dirty ) to prevent the Linux kernel from dropping the storage into a read-only state ( ro,errors=remount-ro ). Under an isolated Linux environment, attached the split Dynfilefs container via @mount.dynfilefs to access the underlying 48 GB virtual block device ( virtual.dat ), mounted the loop target to replay uncommitted XFS journal transactions, and ran xfs_repair -f to resolve dinode CRC corruption (clearing corrupted inode 84628709 , reconstructing allocation group headers, and correcting orphan link counts). Verified a clean zero-error pass across all seven repair phases, unmounted and synced FUSE and loop devices, and executed a clean software ejection via the Windows Shell COM API to ensure safe normal boot readiness.

Reconfigured the Cinnamon power plugin ( csd-power ) and X11 Display Power Management Signaling ( xset +dpms dpms 300 300 300 ) to enforce an automatic 5-minute (300-second) screen turn-off on both AC and battery power, while persistently disabling automatic system suspend on inactivity ( sleep-inactive-*-timeout 0 , type nothing ) to keep long-running processes, local models, and network connections active. To overcome the laptop firmware's minimum hardware PWM backlight floor in Cinnamon Power Management, deployed a persistent software brightness pipeline ( xrandr --output eDP --brightness 0.50 ) via set-screen-brightness.sh , desktop autostart, ~/.xsessionrc , and ~/.xprofile . Furthermore, enabled Cinnamon's native astronomical Night Light daemon ( csd-color ) in automatic schedule mode, calculating real-time local sunset and sunrise coordinates to smoothly transition the display to maximum warmth (1700K color temperature) overnight.

content: With assistance from Antigravity CLI, diagnosed and resolved an unmountable external storage volume on the Windows workstation (Sabrent 500 GB USB SSD / ONETB , mapped as Y: ). The drive failed to mount in File Explorer with Error 1005 ( “The volume does not contain a recognized file system” ) following an incomplete formatting interruption. Leveraged low-level Python Windows API disk I/O to inspect raw volume sectors, discovering that Sector 0 (Volume Boot Record) had been partially overwritten with an invalid EXFAT signature (zeroed checksums and missing cluster heap tables), triggering kernel rejections under exfat.sys . Read the volume geometry and verified that the secondary NTFS Backup Boot Record at the end of the partition remained completely intact ( \xebR\x90NTFS ), confirmed the Master File Table ( $MFT ) at cluster 3, and validated all 35,072 file records (including VirtualBox/VMware virtual machine disks and game archives). Created an offline safety image of Sector 0 and restored the clean 512-byte NTFS boot record using FSCTL_LOCK_VOLUME , WriteFile , and FSCTL_DISMOUNT_VOLUME , instantly remounting Y: with 480 GB of healthy NTFS data and zero file corruption. Diagnosed a lingering ghost drive entry in File Explorer ( ONETB (G:) ) caused by Windows Portable Device shell enumerator ( WPDBUSENUM ) registration and Explorer navigation pane delegate caching, clearing the ghost entry by restarting the Explorer shell.

content: Compared the partition map and filesystem as separate compatibility checks. The 1 TB drive used exFAT, which first raised a filesystem question, but XP Disk Management showed a GPT Protective Partition. That was the stronger clue: XP could see the physical disk and its capacity but did not mount a supported volume, so the barrier came before Explorer and before exFAT. A different file manager would not fix a partition map XP could not read. Microsoft documents the GPT limitation in 32-bit Windows XP .

content: Unity WebGL runtime analysis, WebAssembly delivery triage, and isolated offline execution: With assistance from Antigravity CLI, analyzed the client-side delivery pipeline and runtime execution mechanics of compiled Unity WebGL applications to evaluate self-hosting and deployment constraints on static web architectures. Profiled browser execution under Safari and Chromium DevTools to isolate common runtime startup and scene-transition failures. Identified critical server-side header requirements where Brotli ( .br ) and Gzip ( .gz / .unityweb ) compressed WebAssembly binaries and asset packs fail to compile or unpack on static web hosts lacking custom HTTP Content-Encoding header support . Documented browser CORS protocol boundaries where WebAssembly streaming compilation and binary fetches are blocked under the file:// protocol, requiring a lightweight local HTTP daemon ( python3 -m http.server ) or custom reverse-proxy headers for local testing. Furthermore, diagnosed and stripped legacy third-party analytics hooks and interstitial ad wrappers that intercepted Unity scene switches, preventing offline engine hangs on map loading and canvas initialization. Assembled a multi-application offline WebGL testbed and navigation hub to evaluate WebAssembly heap sizing ( TOTAL_MEMORY allocation ), browser memory limits, and canvas rendering performance across desktop environments. Key Speaking Points & Real-World Analogies: Why double-clicking file:// fails (The Security Guard): Browsers treat local files as isolated origins and block streaming binary fetches; running a lightweight local daemon like python3 -m http.server provides the required HTTP origin.

Identified halted Windows Installer background service states, unregistered OLE/COM handlers, and corrupted Automatic Updates transaction databases. Authored an automated batch repair suite ( reset_xp_update_cache.bat staged on ONEFIVE-XP ) that cleanly stopped wuauserv , bits , cryptsvc , and msiserver , purged corrupt SoftwareDistribution and catroot2 datastores, re-registered ~33 core crypto, OLE, and installer system DLLs via regsvr32 , restored the MSI COM server registration ( msiexec /regserver ), and triggered an immediate Automatic Updates authorization handshake ( wuauclt /resetauthorization /detectnow ) to re-establish clean synchronization with Legacy Update.

Extracted protocol hierarchy and conversation telemetry to map dominant transport endpoints (72% UDP/QUIC, 28% TCP/TLS) without requiring an active graphical Wireshark session.

content: From-scratch neural sequence predictor & in-browser CPU training: With assistance from Antigravity CLI, designed, trained, and deployed an end-to-end custom deep neural network and interactive machine learning laboratory ( ai-predictor.html , css/coin-predictor.css , scripts/coin-predictor.js , and projects.html ). Formulated sequential Bernoulli outcome prediction (coin flips) as a 14-dimensional feature learning task modeling sliding history windows, streak lengths, heads ratios, alternation frequencies, and transition probabilities. Trained a multi-layer perceptron (14 → 32 → 16 → 1) with ReLU activations and Sigmoid classification strictly on CPU using PyTorch 2.13 and Binary Cross-Entropy loss over 100 epochs, driving loss down from 0.6898 to 0.6408 and achieving 54.65% holdout accuracy (+4.65% over pure 50.0% random baseline) by capitalizing on human alternation bias (Gambler's Fallacy) and Diaconis 3D precession physics. Exported model parameters into a zero-dependency client-side JavaScript tensor engine featuring 3D animated coin flip physics, auto-streaming simulations (5 flips/sec), real-time Shannon entropy metrics, interactive loss and accuracy convergence charts, and an in-browser backpropagation engine enabling visitors to train and adapt the model live on their own CPU.

Diagnosed a scenario where the dedicated NVIDIA RTX A2000 Laptop GPU is pinned at 100% compute with 3.95 GB / 4.0 GB VRAM consumed by active ACE-Step 1.5 LoRA training, but the LM Studio service process was still responding over the Tailscale model tunnel, causing the gateway to erroneously advertise status: "online" . Upgraded collect_portfolio_telemetry() to evaluate free GPU VRAM and model load states in real time: if free VRAM is under 2,000 MB or the model is unloaded while the GPU is under load, the gateway flags the system as status: "busy" (HTTP 503) and rejects incoming generation requests with an explicit retry notice. Configured scripts/script.js to dynamically hide the floating “Chat with Nemo” launcher across the entire site and lock the telemetry action on stats.html to “AI Node Busy • Training”, completely protecting active training runs from CUDA Out of Memory (OOM) faults.

title: Autonomous Drive C Forensics & Precision Reclamation: Reclaiming 65+ GB on Windows with Antigravity AI
snippet: Autonomous Drive C Forensics & Precision Reclamation: Reclaiming 65+ GB on Windows with Antigravity AI In Progress Parallel File Tree Forensics · Reparse Point Auditing · PyTorch Checkpoint Pruning · Antigravity AI Pair Programming · Active October 28, 2026 Ho...
content: Autonomous Drive C Forensics & Precision Reclamation: Reclaiming 65+ GB on Windows with Antigravity AI In Progress Parallel File Tree Forensics · Reparse Point Auditing · PyTorch Checkpoint Pruning · Antigravity AI Pair Programming · Active October 28, 2026 How systematic parallel filesystem inspection with Google DeepMind's Antigravity AI diagnosed a critical 93.2% capacity bottleneck on my primary Windows SSD, recovered over 65 GB in safe multi-stage sweeps, and established a zero-loss roadmap to reclaim 40+ GB more. The Capacity Wall: 93.2% Full on Primary Drive C As a developer running local machine learning fine-tuning, multiple virtualization platforms, and containerized dev environments on a primary workstation, disk storage is constantly under high pressure. On October 28, 2026, my primary 500 GB NVMe solid-state drive ( C:\ ) hit a critical threshold: Total Capacity: 475.93 GB Used Space: 443.74 GB ( 93.2% capacity ) Free Space Remaining: Only 32.19 GB With an active PyTorch fine-tuning workflow producing multi-epoch checkpoints, multiple VM disk images, and heavy developer caching, running below 35 GB of headroom created immediate risks of filesystem thrashing, aborted training epochs, and broken Windows virtual memory paging. I needed a systematic, zero-data-loss storage audit to pinpoint exactly what was eating the drive and safely reclaim tens of gigabytes without disrupting running environments. Algorithmic Filesystem Forensics: Eliminating Recursion & Junction Traps Standard Windows tools like File Explorer and naive PowerShell recursive commands ( Get-ChildItem -Recurse ) quickly proved unusable for a drive this large: they either froze indefinitely, spawned millions of .NET object allocations that devoured system RAM, or got trapped in infinite recursion loops caused by Windows filesystem junctions (such as the legacy Application Data loop pointing back into AppData\Local ). To solve this, I paired up with Antigravity , Google DeepMind's agentic AI coding assistant. Operating directly in my workstation terminal through autonomous PowerShell and Python execution harnesses, Antigravity built a high-speed multi-threaded filesystem crawler that bypassed standard pitfalls: Low-Level Reparse Point Detection: Inspected the Win32 file attribute bitmask ( st_file_attributes & 0x400 ) to identify and safely bypass directory junctions and cloud-reparse placeholders (preventing infinite loops and unwanted OneDrive file hydration). Concurrent Multi-Worker Directory Walks: Leveraged Python's ThreadPoolExecutor with 8 parallel worker threads using os.scandir directly against Windows NT filesystem APIs, scanning hundreds of thousands of files across deep subtrees in seconds. The forensic scan revealed the primary storage offenders across Drive C: C:\Users\Owner : 232.93 GB (over 52.5% of the entire drive), dominated by AppData (73.6 GB), Downloads (56.4 GB), AI_Apps (19.3 GB), and VirtualBox VMs (21.2 GB). C:\ProgramData : 20.23 GB , heavily consumed by a 13.88 GB BlueStacks Android emulator container. C:\Windows : 55.63 GB , including 20.4 GB in WinSxS and a massive 15.0 GB in System32\DriverStore (accumulated superseded driver packages). Root System Files: 18.92 GB locked by hiberfil.sys (12.67 GB) and pagefile.sys (6.25 GB). Phase 1: What We Have Cleaned Up (+65.10 GB Reclaimed) Working collaboratively through interactive planning, we executed an incremental, safe series of surgical purges: Slax Linux Session Backups & Build Artifacts (7.54 GB Physical Reclaim): Permanently removed slax_session1_backup (which held multiple multi-gigabyte sparse changes.dat.* persistence files) and Slax-build (custom ISO outputs like slax-debian-xfce-custom.iso and Slackware module archives). FreeBSD VirtualBox VM Decommissioning (3.18 GB): Cleanly unregistered the powered-off VM using Oracle's CLI tool: & "C:\Program Files\Oracle\VirtualBox\VBoxManage.exe" unregistervm "FreeBSD 64 bits" --delete This safely purged the virtual disk ( FreeBSD 64 bits.vdi ) and configuration without leaving orphaned entries in the VirtualBox machine registry. Orphaned Kali VM Snapshot Removal (5.31 GB): The audit detected an orphaned 4.11 GB saved state snapshot ( 2026-09-13...sav ) in VirtualBox VMs\Kali 64 BITS\Snapshots belonging to a VM that was no longer registered in VirtualBox, safely eliminating it while leaving active VMs (such as 458project ) completely untouched. Deep Dive on PyTorch LoRA Resumption & Checkpoint Pruning (35.0 GB): My Downloads/ACE_STEP_Dataset_Clean_30s directory held over 51 GB of training outputs across multiple runs. I wanted to verify whether deleting early epoch checkpoints would break my ability to resume training from later checkpoints. Together with Antigravity, we inspected my training scripts ( resume_training_to_epoch100.py and train.py ) and verified that every checkpoint directory is 100% self-contained : adapter_model.safetensors (84 MB) stores the complete cumulative LoRA weights up to that epoch. training_state.pt (168.3 MB) contains the complete AdamW optimizer momentum buffers, learning rate scheduler state, and global step count. When resuming training via --resume-from <checkpoint_dir> , PyTorch loads strictly from that target folder and never references earlier epochs. With this confirmed, we performed an extensive pruning sweep: Deleted obsolete early run lora_output_validated_epoch45 ( 7.48 GB ). Deleted obsolete run lora_output_validated_epoch100 ( 9.94 GB ). Deleted 8 miscellaneous early test runs (epochs 1, 4, 6, 7, 12, 25, 60, and continuation tests, reclaiming 7.97 GB ). Pruned 39 intermediate checkpoints from lora_output_validated_epoch180 while preserving epoch_180_loss_0.8729 and the exported final adapter for future audio sound benchmarking (reclaiming 9.61 GB ). BlueStacks Android Container Purge (13.88 GB): Permanently removed C:\ProgramData\BlueStacks_nxt , wiping unused Android VHD virtual disks and cache. OneDrive Local Cache Dehydration: Executed attrib +U -P /s /d across duplicate GGUF models ( Z3. LM Studio Models ) and portable app runtimes in OneDrive - Grand Valley State University (1) to instruct OneDrive's Cloud Files engine to evict local disk sectors while preserving cloud availability. Phase 1 Result: Free disk space on Drive C expanded from 32.19 GB to 97.29 GB —a net recovery of 65.10 GB of high-speed NVMe storage , bringing drive capacity down from 93.2% to 79.5% . Phase 2: In-Progress Roadmap (Identified Targets for 40+ GB More) Because this project is active and ongoing, we cataloged and staged the next batch of high-yield reclamation targets to execute in subsequent pair-programming sessions: Prune Intermediate Checkpoints in Epoch 200 (~4.75 GB): Apply the same surgical pruning to lora_output_validated_epoch200 —preserving our all-time lowest loss checkpoint ( epoch_200_loss_0.8885 , step 4,600) and the final adapter while clearing intermediate epochs 181–199. Orphaned Windows 11 VM Snapshot (5.51 GB): Remove VirtualBox VMs\Windows 11\Snapshots\2026-09-13...sav (an orphaned saved-state file from an unregistered VM with no base disk). Python Package Wheels & Build Caches (11.1 GB): Run uv cache clean ( 8.0 GB ) and pip cache purge ( 3.1 GB ) in AppData\Local to wipe downloaded package archives without affecting any installed virtual environment. User Temp Scratches (4.18 GB): Purge scratch installers and crash logs in AppData\Local\Temp . Academic Lab Forensics Image (7.0 GB): Archive Documents\cis430\lab05\evidence\InCh05.img (6.0 GB raw forensic dump) to external homelab cold storage. Disable Windows Fast Startup / Hibernation (12.67 GB): Execute powercfg /h off from an elevated administrator command prompt to permanently remove C:\hiberfil.sys . WSL2 Debian Virtual Disk Compaction (up to 15 GB): Run diskpart compaction against AppData\Local\wsl\...\ext4.vhdx (currently 24.1 GB on host while only 19 GB is used internally). Session Telemetry & Resuming with Antigravity AI To ensure continuity and reproducibility across sessions, the entire investigation trajectory, environment state, and diagnostic tooling are maintained in Google DeepMind's Antigravity assistant system. Antigravity CLI Conversation ID: 362b53f1-3a98-4019-bde4-e886b81f209a How to Resume This Project Session: From any terminal on the workstation running Antigravity CLI, run: agy --resume 362b53f1-3a98-4019-bde4-e886b81f209a Or open the Antigravity session manager and select this conversation to continue directly from the current filesystem state.

title: Cross-Volume Archive Deduplication & Dual-Drive Mirroring: Deconstructing Google Takeout with Antigravity AI
snippet: Cross-Volume Archive Deduplication & Dual-Drive Mirroring: Deconstructing Google Takeout with Antigravity AI Completed Project Tailscale SMB · exFAT vs. NTFS Delta Sync · PowerShell Forensics · Antigravity AI Pair Programming · Completed October 28, 2026 How p...
content: Cross-Volume Archive Deduplication & Dual-Drive Mirroring: Deconstructing Google Takeout with Antigravity AI Completed Project Tailscale SMB · exFAT vs. NTFS Delta Sync · PowerShell Forensics · Antigravity AI Pair Programming · Completed October 28, 2026 How pair programming with Google DeepMind's Antigravity AI turned a 70 GB nested Google Takeout maze and network sync bottleneck into an automated, zero-data-loss storage audit and 5-minute smart delta sync. The Storage Sprawl Dilemma: Multi-Part Takeout & Fragmented Roots Over years of backups, data sprawl is inevitable. Across my homelab storage array—specifically drive B:\ ( ONEFIVE , a 500 GB NTFS partition hosted on my stationary Alpine Linux NUC and accessed remotely via Tailscale authenticated SMB) and drive G:\ ( ONETB , a 1 TB high-capacity local exFAT drive)—both root filesystems contained a legacy folder named Z4. Drive Takeout . Google Takeout exports are notoriously unwieldy: multi-part zip archives unpack into nested folder trees four to six levels deep ( Z4. Drive Takeout\avanek2005\takeout-20260510T175627Z-3-001\takeout-...\Takeout\Drive\05. All backups\... ). Compounding the confusion, previous partial extractions had left fragmented remnants scattered across the root directories of both drives—including loose files in 23. driveRootFilez , folders like 05. Backups , and raw timestamped export names like 02. Counseling Stuff-20260517T221837Z-3-001 . Simply wiping Z4. Drive Takeout was out of the question: blindly deleting 25,600+ files (~70 GB) carried massive risks of permanently destroying unique personal documents, irreplaceable family concert footage, or unindexed photo albums. Yet manually verifying and sorting every nested directory by hand would have required days of mind-numbing clicking. Algorithmic File Forensics: Pairing with Antigravity AI To eliminate the guesswork and ensure strict zero data loss, I paired up with Antigravity , Google DeepMind's agentic AI coding assistant. Operating directly in the environment through automated PowerShell inspection harnesses, Antigravity systematically indexed, cataloged, and cross-referenced all 25,616 files in Z4. Drive Takeout against the root directory contents of both drives. The forensic audit categorized the 69.64 GB archive into four distinct actionable buckets: Safe Movie Pruning (“Yoinking” 2.62 GB): In takeout-003 , the audit isolated two large movies ( PLANES_FIRE_AND_RESCUE [828 MB] and The_APPLE_DUMPLING_GANG [1.98 GB]). Cross-referencing against G:\09. Movies\PG+G Movies\ proved they were 100% byte-for-byte identical duplicates, allowing them to be safely deleted immediately. Promoting 58 GB of Google Photos: The audit discovered that Takeout\Google Photos held 25,308 files (~58 GB) with zero representation anywhere on the root of either drive. Deleting the Takeout folder would have wiped out the entire photo library. Instead, we executed an instant filesystem rename, promoting the directory directly to root as 03. Google Photos on both drives (taking 0 extra bytes and 0 seconds). Rescuing Loose Root Documents (304 MB): Nine loose Google Drive documents and videos (including a 292 MB recording 20210119_021608A.mp4 , study audio, and presentations) were extracted and consolidated directly into 23. driveRootFilez . Recovering Irreplaceable Backups & Photo Sets (8.96 GB): Deep inside 05. All backups , the audit surfaced five irreplaceable family concert and anniversary videos (6.5 GB from 2012–2017) that existed nowhere else on any drive, plus 290 phone picture backups. These were safely migrated and merged into 05. Backups without overwriting existing files. Once every byte was accounted for and safely housed, Z4. Drive Takeout was completely empty and permanently deleted from both drives. Overcoming SMB Protocol & exFAT vs. NTFS Timestamp Roadblocks With the archive cleared, the next step was bringing B:\ and G:\ into clean mirror synchronization (excluding designated local folders _TEMP on B: and 09. Movies on G: ). However, standard Windows utilities immediately surfaced low-level filesystem incompatibilities: SMB Error 50 ( The request is not supported ): Standard tools like robocopy and xcopy attempting to preserve POSIX directory attributes over the remote Tailscale SMB mount failed because the underlying Linux Samba share rejects certain Windows directory attribute modifications. We adapted the tooling to handle data streams cleanly without triggering attribute errors. The exFAT Timestamp Resolution Trap: When running standard delta sync ( xcopy /D ), the process stalled on 19. WiiU stuf (a 44.8 GB directory) and began re-copying a 14.36 GB archive over the Wi-Fi link. The cause: G:\ is formatted as exFAT (which rounds timestamps to 2-second increments), while B:\ is NTFS (sub-second precision). Standard timestamp comparison falsely flagged identical multi-gigabyte ISOs as “newer” on NTFS, threatening to drag out the sync for over 3 hours across 150+ GB of already-identical game dumps. Engineering the Smart Delta Sync: Hours to 5 Minutes Rather than letting network transfers waste hours re-streaming identical files, we terminated the brute-force transfer and engineered a targeted PowerShell Smart-Sync engine ( smart_sync.ps1 ). The script used existence checks and strict byte-length comparison rather than fragile cross-filesystem timestamps, completely skipping the 150+ GB of verified Wii, Wii U, and ROM archives. The smart engine executed in roughly 5 minutes, targeting only true discrepancies: Transferred 542 missing songs into 00. All Music Playlists Revamped LOCAL (bringing both drives to an identical 41.86 GB audio corpus). Synchronized developer software packages (MySQL macOS/Windows installers, Android x86 ISOs, and IPA archives) between drives in 08 Software . Mirrored OpenVPN profiles, Minecraft server configurations, and Windows XP legacy wallpapers. Normalized takeout suffix folders on G:\ (e.g., 02. Counseling Stuff and 04. Personal Portfolio Website Stuff ) to match B:\ . A post-sync verification audit confirmed 100% parity across all shared directories on both drives, transforming an intimidating, confusing archive sprawl into an organized, fully redundant storage architecture.

title: One Assistant, Two Brains: Self-Updating AI Assistant on Google Cloud
snippet: One Assistant, Two Brains: Self-Updating AI Assistant on Google Cloud Live & Deployed Cloud Run · Vertex AI Agent Builder · SharePoint REST API · Updated October 22, 2026 How a “can I just add a bot in Teams?” idea became a self-updating AI assistant on Google...
content: One Assistant, Two Brains: Self-Updating AI Assistant on Google Cloud Live & Deployed Cloud Run · Vertex AI Agent Builder · SharePoint REST API · Updated October 22, 2026 How a “can I just add a bot in Teams?” idea became a self-updating AI assistant on Google Cloud — conceived on a Tuesday, live by Wednesday night. The idea It started with a simple want: a chatbot I could message like a person. I work at the GVSU IT Service Desk, where I answer the same questions over and over — how to register a game console on the dorm network, where a form lives, what laptop a computing student should buy — and my “system” for that knowledge was a stack of bookmarks and KB articles I could never find fast enough. At the same time I’m a student, and my coursework lived in a OneDrive folder of hundreds of files: lecture notes, transcripts, screenshots, worksheets, study guides. None of it searchable as a whole. So: one assistant with two brains. My service-desk knowledge for work, my class materials for studying — and a switch to choose which brain answers. I designed the switch to sit right by the message input, like ChatGPT’s model picker: Service Desk / Classes / Everything. First direction: Microsoft Teams (and why it died) The original plan was a Teams bot I could add like a contact. Research killed it quickly: personal Teams can’t sideload custom bots as contacts, and Zoom bots aren’t contacts either. I also already had a half-built Teams bot sitting in Google Cloud from an earlier attempt — it answered every message with a 503 error, because its Microsoft credentials were never configured. On October 21 I scrapped Teams and Azure entirely: Google Cloud would be the brain, a simple web page would be the face. The simplest thing that could possibly work. What got built A web chat app (Python/Flask on Google Cloud Run) with the mode switcher by the input, and answers that cite their sources A Vertex AI Agent Builder (Discovery Engine) search engine combining two data stores, with generative summaries Brain one — Service Desk: 649 GVSU IT knowledge-base documents Brain two — Classes: ~977 documents synced from my OneDrive class folders to Cloud Storage, updated automatically A daily sync job (Cloud Run Job triggered by Cloud Scheduler at 3 AM) that walks the OneDrive folder tree via SharePoint’s REST API, downloads new/changed files, generates a dynamic course-list index, and replaces the corpus in Cloud Storage The problems that made it interesting The 1-store limit Agent Builder can search multiple data stores in one engine — but only if you choose “Generic” at engine-creation time. Pick anything else and it silently locks the engine to a single store forever. Caught this before writing code by testing the console first; rebuilt the engine as Generic so Service Desk and Classes could share one brain. The OneDrive sync marathon Connecting to GVSU OneDrive without admin consent (which would make the official routes painful) meant using the folder’s anyone-with-the-link sharing through SharePoint’s REST API directly — proven with a server-side test first. The sync then failed in stages, each diagnosed from logs: deep folder recursion hit SharePoint errors; the folder walk had to be hardened (loop protection, depth caps, per-folder error recording); then it ran out of memory at Cloud Run’s default; then it outgrew the 15-minute web-request timeout — so it was re-platformed from a web service into a background job with an hour-long window. That run succeeded: 403 folders, 1,937 files walked, 1,024 documents transferred, zero errors. The apostrophe bug Two folders kept failing. Root cause: their names contain apostrophes (“THis Week’s Lecture Screenshots”), which break the single-quoted path format in SharePoint’s API. Escaping the quotes fixed the last two folders. The martial-arts incident With coursework imported, I asked the bot “What classes am I taking?” — and it confidently described a Martial Arts Academy’s schedule. Kids 6–12, adults 13+, black-belt instructors. It had retrieved my CIS 460 coursework, which is full of a textbook case study about a martial arts academy — and no document in the pile actually listed my courses. Retrieval was working; the corpus had a hole in it. The fix became a design principle: the sync now generates the course list from my actual folder names every night , so the answer is derived from reality and can’t rot. The silent summarizer Even then, Classes mode wouldn’t produce summaries — just Google’s canned “A summary could not be generated.” Controlled API probes (same question against different stores, same store with different request shapes) isolated it: the platform’s summarizer classifies my classes store as “out of domain” and refuses, full stop. Rather than fight it, the chat app now detects a skipped summary and composes the answer from the documents’ own text excerpts — arguably more trustworthy, since it’s quoting my files. (A parser bug in that fallback was caught by testing against realistic data objects instead of friendly mocks — a lesson that stuck.) The guardrail The chat is public by design, so the last piece was the $10 budget alert: if the project ever spends $5 in a month, I get an email. It normally spends $0.00. What it does today Ask it what classes I’m taking: “CIS 430, CIS 450, CIS 457, CIS 460” — from the generated course list. Ask what my study guide says to focus on: it quotes my own notes (probable cause, the third-party doctrine…). Ask how to register a device on the dorm network: the full service-desk walkthrough, help-desk number included, KB articles cited. Every night at 3 AM it re-syncs itself, so this week’s lecture screenshots are just… in there. Total running cost so far: $0.00 , against a $1,000 trial credit. What I took from it Platform constraints are design inputs, not surprises — if you probe them early (single-store engines, tenant restrictions, timeout ceilings). Derive indexes from reality. Hand-maintained pointer documents rot; a course list regenerated from the folder tree nightly can’t. Debug with receipts: change one variable, read the platform’s own error, write it down. Every failure above had a specific, boring, fixable cause. Security is a dial, not a switch: public + monitored + budget-capped was the right setting for a tool whose whole value is zero-friction access at work. Stack Google Cloud Run Cloud Scheduler Cloud Storage Vertex AI Agent Builder / Discovery Engine Python (Flask) SharePoint REST API HTML/CSS GitHub + Cloudflare (this site) Try it live: The assistant is active on this site — open the AI assistant chat and ask it something. AI collaboration credit: Built with Muse, Meta’s AI assistant, as a pair-programming and infrastructure partner across two very long days in October 2026.

title: GVSU IT Service Desk: AI-Assisted Chatbot Workflow Testing
snippet: GVSU IT Service Desk: AI-Assisted Chatbot Workflow Testing Follow-up in Progress Initial testing & documentation complete · Six test runs · Updated October 20, 2026 During my work at the Grand Valley State University IT Service Desk, I evaluated a support chat...
content: GVSU IT Service Desk: AI-Assisted Chatbot Workflow Testing Follow-up in Progress Initial testing & documentation complete · Six test runs · Updated October 20, 2026 During my work at the Grand Valley State University IT Service Desk, I evaluated a support chatbot in a sandbox environment. I focused on whether it could recognize an account-access problem, verify the account holder, and continue into its password-reset capability without requiring the user to name the internal workflow. Testing the conversation, not just the happy path I worked with OpenAI’s ChatGPT/Codex across six test runs, including a restart attempt and fresh incognito sessions. Scenarios covered ordinary forgotten-password requests, corrections, malformed input, requests to skip verification, and help requested on someone else’s behalf. I supplied the service-desk context, clarified the expected procedures, and selected the account-verification answers; Codex operated the browser and helped capture observations and organize the evidence. Turning unexpected behavior into useful evidence The tests surfaced inconsistent routing, repeated requests for information already supplied, and handoffs that did not follow the expected service-desk process. Two runs reached a reported successful verification and then a reported failure during the reset attempt. I kept those observations separate from assumptions about the underlying cause: a chatbot’s explanation is useful evidence, but staff need backend logs and configuration access to establish what happened. I preserved native chat transcripts, added notes describing the purpose and limitations of each run, and organized the results into two review packages with summary reports. This made it possible to distinguish repeatable problems from test-input issues and expected behavior, such as changing the order of identity-verification questions. Current progress and next steps The initial testing and documentation phase is complete, and I am continuing the follow-up. My next steps are to share the findings with professional staff, clarify expected behavior with the responsible team, and support their investigation with the recorded test conditions. Backend investigation and fixes remain with that team. After changes are available, I plan to repeat the affected scenarios and document whether the verification-to-reset flow and account-holder handoff behave as expected. This project is strengthening my approach to quality assurance: test realistic user intent, check recovery paths, preserve reproducible evidence, and be precise about what a test does and does not prove. AI collaboration credit: OpenAI’s ChatGPT/Codex assisted with browser-based testing, note-taking, and report packaging under my direction. I provided the workplace knowledge and policy guidance. This write-up describes my contribution and does not represent an official GVSU statement.

content: Secure Out-of-Network Printing & Device Reverse Proxy via Tailscale on Alpine Linux Completed Project Remote IPP/RAW print relay & trusted HTTPS management verified · Completed October 19, 2026 I engineered persistent out-of-network printing to my home HP OfficeJet 5200 series all-in-one printer and eliminated browser security warnings for my TP-Link Archer AX3000 router management using an always-on Alpine Linux NUC over Tailscale. The solution enables seamless printing and trusted administrative access from macOS, Windows, Linux, and iOS without exposing internal devices to the public internet or requiring open WAN ports. Remote client on Tailscale → Alpine NUC (100.87.81.52) → SNI TLS & Header Rewrite → LAN Printer / Router (192.168.0.x) The Discovery & Routing Breakdown While my home router was accessible remotely via an existing Tailscale subnet route ( 192.168.0.0/24 ), printing away from home consistently failed. Investigating the network exchange revealed two structural barriers: Windows installs printers by default using Web Services for Devices (WSD), and Apple devices rely on AirPrint (mDNS / Bonjour). Both protocols depend on link-local multicast (UDP 3702 and 5353) which cannot cross VPN subnet boundaries, causing remote clients to flag the printer as offline. Furthermore, traveling to guest networks or hotels that also utilize 192.168.0.0/24 causes local subnet collisions where outbound traffic never enters the Tailscale tunnel. To achieve deterministic access anywhere in the world, the printer and management services needed to be directly anchored to the NUC's static CGNAT Tailscale address ( 100.87.81.52 ). Building the Persistent Multi-Protocol Relay On the Alpine Linux NUC, I implemented an asynchronous Python relay service ( printer-relay ) supervised under OpenRC with supervise-daemon . To prevent public internet exposure, all listeners bind strictly to the private Tailscale interface: Port 9100 (RAW / JetDirect): Direct socket streaming for high-speed, driver-native printing across Windows, macOS, and Linux. Port 631 (IPP / IPPS): Standard Internet Printing Protocol relay supporting modern IPP Everywhere print queues and mobile printing apps. Port 9080 (HTTP) & Port 9444 (HTTPS): Reverse proxy for the HP Embedded Web Server (EWS), enabling remote ink telemetry, diagnostics, and scanner access. Port 9445 (Router HTTPS): Dedicated reverse proxy for the TP-Link router management portal. Dynamic LAN Failover: Rather than relying solely on a hardcoded IP, the relay actively queries the home LAN over mDNS ( _ipp._tcp.local ) to track the printer dynamically if its DHCP lease rotates. Overcoming DNS Rebinding & Self-Signed Certificate Warnings Accessing the printer's Embedded Web Server revealed an upstream firmware defense: HP's internal nginx server enforces strict DNS Rebinding protection, returning 403 Forbidden whenever incoming HTTP Host headers do not match the printer's local address. The relay transparently rewrites the HTTP Host header to 192.168.0.181 and rewrites downstream Location redirects back to the client. Similarly, the TP-Link router defaults to a self-signed certificate issued to CN=tplinkwifi.net . Browsing to https://192.168.0.1/ caused browsers (Firefox, Chrome, Safari) to strike a red line through HTTPS and display persistent “Your connection is not private” warnings, forcing tedious manual bypasses whenever cache cleared. I eliminated all browser security warnings by provisioning trusted TLS using Tailscale's Let's Encrypt certificates with Server Name Indication (SNI) on ports 9444 and 9445. Navigating to https://nucwol2-0--hdd.taile72a68.ts.net:9444 (printer) and https://nucwol2-0--hdd.taile72a68.ts.net:9445 (router) delivers a verified green padlock with zero SSL warnings, allowing administrative updates, firmware checks, and router configuration without security prompts. Client Verification I verified end-to-end printing and telemetry across multiple client operating systems by mapping standard TCP/IP queues to 100.87.81.52:9100 on Windows and macOS. The OpenRC service was added to the default boot runlevel, confirming full persistence across system reboots.

title: Homelab / Retro computing!
snippet: Homelab / Retro computing! In Progress Vintage Windows XP Integration · Updated October 25, 2026 I enjoy working across different computing eras and exploring how legacy hardware and modern networks interact. As part of my homelab experiments, I brought a vint...
content: Homelab / Retro computing! In Progress Vintage Windows XP Integration · Updated October 25, 2026 I enjoy working across different computing eras and exploring how legacy hardware and modern networks interact. As part of my homelab experiments, I brought a vintage Windows XP machine onto my network to serve as a retro workstation and testing node. Integrating a quarter-century-old operating system into a modern infrastructure ecosystem highlights both the durability of early-2000s software and the technical hurdles required to bridge modern security standards with legacy protocols. Solving the modern-to-legacy SSH protocol gap Modern OpenSSH client implementations (like those default in current versions of macOS and Linux) intentionally disable older, deprecated cryptographic primitives such as ssh-rsa (SHA-1 signatures) and legacy ciphers due to security vulnerabilities. Meanwhile, legacy Windows SSH daemons—in this case, freeSSHd running on the WeOnlyDo 2.4.3 backend—only negotiate these older standards. Attempting a standard connection immediately failed during host key exchange. Rather than degrading global system security, I isolated host-specific cryptographic compatibility rules in my client SSH configuration ( ~/.ssh/config ). Explicitly re-enabling HostKeyAlgorithms +ssh-rsa , PubkeyAcceptedKeyTypes +ssh-rsa , and fallback key exchange methods permitted the client to negotiate securely with the XP host while keeping the rest of my workstation strictly bound to modern cipher standards. Debugging the “Could not find window” console hook error Once the SSH cryptographic handshake succeeded and credentials were authenticated, the connection abruptly terminated with an obscure message: Could not find window of executed program. Connection closed. Diagnosing this required understanding how early Windows console hosting functioned prior to modern ConPTY architectures. Tools like freeSSHd execute cmd.exe and attempt to enumerate and hook into the program's console window to scrape output and redirect keystrokes. Because the daemon was initially running as a background Windows Service, Windows XP's service session isolation prevented it from acquiring a visible interactive desktop handle or window context for the spawned process. I resolved this by transitioning freeSSHd away from the headless system service model and running it as an interactive application within the active user desktop session (minimized to the system tray and configured to launch at user startup). Instantly, the console scraper bound successfully, yielding a full interactive C:\Documents and Settings\avanek> command prompt remotely over SSH. Architecting resilient 41 GB file sync: Native XCOPY & strict SMB isolation The next phase involved transferring a 41 GB curated audio archive to a secondary storage partition ( F:\00. All Music Playlists Revamped LOCAL ) on the XP machine. Pushing 41 GB over freeSSHd was impractical due to memory leaks and socket hangs when the machine's vintage USB Wi-Fi dongle dropped connection. Instead, I leveraged my stationary Alpine Linux NUC, which already had the source drive mounted locally at /media/onefive . Rather than exposing SMB promiscuously to the local network or mixing legacy protocols with modern devices, I maintained strict architectural isolation: The Tailscale Share ( [ONEFIVE] ): Modern devices connect over encrypted Tailscale using authenticated SMB3. Guest access is prohibited. The Isolated XP Share ( [ONEFIVE-XP] ): Configured as a guest-only SMB1 (NT1) share pointing to the same media mount, strictly locked down at two independent layers: an OpenRC nftables firewall guard ( smb-tailscale-firewall ) dropping all LAN port 445 traffic, and Samba's internal hosts allow directive. Investigating access revealed that a DHCP lease shift had reassigned the XP machine from .160 to .161 , triggering the firewall guard. Updating the nftables filter and Samba configuration allowed the XP machine to connect to \\192.168.0.201\ONEFIVE-XP . When Windows XP prompted for credentials because the client username matched a local Linux user account, connecting with the guest principal and an empty password completed the handshake successfully without requiring account credentials. Before automating the sync, migrating files had been an exercise in pure stubborn persistence: because the USB Wi-Fi adapter frequently dropped connections, I had literally been nursing transfers by manually copying small “blocks” of files at a time. If a large transfer dropped mid-way, the entire batch failed, leaving corrupted partial files and no clear record of what succeeded. With the share mapped to drive Z: , I eliminated manual babysitting by deploying unattended batch scripts ( sync_music.bat , sync_extras.bat , and sync_movies.bat ) directly onto the network mount. The scripts execute native Windows xcopy with delta and fault-tolerance flags ( /E /C /I /Q /H /R /Y /D ) to migrate over 220 GB of archives—including the 41 GB music library, portable ROMs, system backups, cheatsheets, project files, and a ~112 GB video collection—straight onto partition F: . Real-time Samba telemetry on the NUC confirmed active read locks and a steady ~2.6 MB/s stream. To pull the 112 GB video library from a separate modern Windows PC on the local network, I mapped its dedicated storage share as a virtual drive directly within the batch pipeline. The script self-heals by verifying network path availability, reconnecting if disconnected, and preserving transfer state so even massive multi-gigabyte video files can be ingested smoothly onto the XP workstation without babysitting. During overnight migrations, a combination of legacy power-saving quirks and dynamic DHCP lease renewals surfaced: when the display went to sleep or the router reassigned the wireless adapter between .160 and .161 , the active TCP socket dropped with “The network location cannot be reached.” By default, Windows XP aggressively cuts power to USB root hubs and network adapters during display idle. I hardened the workstation by setting the power scheme to “Always On” and disabling power-saving shutoffs on the USB wireless adapter and root hubs in Device Manager. To eliminate manual intervention when transient network renegotiations happen, I consolidated the fragmented tasks into a single master orchestration pipeline ( sync_all.bat ) spanning all 13 archive categories across both hosts (~283 GB total). Because the vintage workstation is situated in an area without direct Ethernet drops, the entire multi-day transfer runs wirelessly over 802.11g at roughly 1.0 to 1.2 MB/s. On a machine with only 256 MB of RAM, sustaining an unattended ~70-hour data migration requires deep resilience: the batch engine continually tests network share reachability, purges stale SMB sessions ( net use Z: /delete /y ), executes ICMP ping backoffs on dropouts, and uses native date comparison ( xcopy /D ) to resume without re-copying existing files. I also implemented graceful PnP device node ejection ( CM_Request_Device_Eject via Windows SetupAPI) on the host to cleanly dismount and swap source storage volumes (including a 1 TB external movie library mapped to Y:\ ) without interrupting the migration loop. Diagnosing the 28 failing .NET updates (Error 0x80070643 / MSI 1601) While maintaining the machine, I encountered a roadblock where a stubborn batch of 28 Windows updates repeatedly failed to install. Rather than guessing in the dark or triggering freeSSHd interactive console crashes, I used non-interactive SSH remote command execution to stream and parse C:\WINDOWS\WindowsUpdate.log directly to my Mac. The log revealed two distinct issues: first, the unstable USB Wi-Fi dongle frequently dropped DNS resolution mid-check ( hr = 80072ee7 / 0x8024402c ). Second, and more importantly, all 28 failing updates were specifically Microsoft .NET Framework (2.0 SP2, 3.0 SP2, and 3.5 SP1) security rollups throwing error 0x80070643 with an underlying return code of 0x00000641 . In Windows system error codes, hexadecimal 0x641 converts to decimal 1601: ERROR_INSTALL_SERVICE_FAILURE (“The Windows Installer Service could not be accessed”). The issue was not corrupted OS binaries, but rather the stock Windows Installer 3.1 engine failing to service modern MSI packages required by the late-era .NET updates. To eliminate this roadblock without needing physical USB drive swaps, I staged the official Windows Installer 4.5 redistributable ( WindowsXP-KB942288-v3-x86.exe ) directly onto the NUC network share, executed the installation on the XP machine, and verified via msiexec that the installer engine successfully upgraded to version 4.5.6001.22159. Even with the updated installer binaries in place, subsequent installation attempts initially threw error 0x00000641 because the MSIServer COM service was halted and the legacy Windows Update datastores had corrupted transaction journals. To permanently resolve this, I authored a comprehensive maintenance automation ( reset_xp_update_cache.bat ) that cleanly stops the Windows Update, BITS, Cryptographic, and MSI services, purges corrupt cache directories ( SoftwareDistribution and catroot2 ), re-registers ~33 core crypto, OLE, and installer DLLs via regsvr32 , repairs the MSI COM server registration ( msiexec /regserver ), and resets client-side update authorization ( wuauclt /resetauthorization /detectnow ). This restored clean communication between Legacy Update and the local installer engine. The POSReady 2009 timeline: Why ATMs kept Windows XP alive until 2019 One of the most fascinating aspects of servicing vintage Windows XP in modern times is watching official security patches with 2018 and 2019 timestamps install on an operating system originally released in 2001. When Microsoft officially ended mainstream consumer support for Windows XP on April 8, 2014, an estimated 95% of the world's automated teller machines (ATMs) and millions of retail point-of-sale (POS) checkout registers were still running on the Windows XP architecture. Upgrading those machines to modern versions of Windows was virtually impossible at the time: ATMs were bolted to complex, proprietary motorized cash feeders, encrypted PIN pads, and check scanners whose 32-bit vendor drivers only functioned on Windows NT 5.1. Furthermore, retail checkout registers were fanless, low-power embedded appliances running on 500 MHz processors with 512 MB of RAM and small 4 GB CompactFlash cards—specs that could never meet Windows 7 or 10 requirements. Because Microsoft had released Windows Embedded POSReady 2009 in late 2008 with a standard 10-year enterprise lifecycle agreement, the company was contractually obligated to engineer, compile, and distribute official security updates and .NET cumulative rollups for the 32-bit NT 5.1 architecture all the way through April 9, 2019. Shortly after consumer XP was retired in 2014, enthusiasts discovered that POSReady 2009 shared the exact same core kernel ( ntoskrnl.exe ), memory manager, and system libraries as Windows XP SP3. By adding a single three-line registry entry ( [HKLM\SYSTEM\WPA\PosReady] "Installed"=dword:00000001 ), standard Windows XP installations could identify as POSReady terminals to Windows Update, unlocking an extra five years of critical enterprise patches. Seeing this vintage 256 MB RAM workstation pull and install those late-era security rollups in 2026 brings an extraordinary chapter of enterprise computing history to life.

title: Cross-Platform Minecraft Server & Zero-Config Global Tunneling: PaperMC 26.3, GeyserMC & Playit.gg Relay
snippet: Cross-Platform Minecraft Server & Zero-Config Global Tunneling: PaperMC 26.3, GeyserMC & Playit.gg Relay Completed Project PaperMC 26.3 · GeyserMC Bedrock Bridge · Playit.gg Tunneling · Socat Relay · Completed October 17, 2026 I wanted to set up a dependable p...
content: Cross-Platform Minecraft Server & Zero-Config Global Tunneling: PaperMC 26.3, GeyserMC & Playit.gg Relay Completed Project PaperMC 26.3 · GeyserMC Bedrock Bridge · Playit.gg Tunneling · Socat Relay · Completed October 17, 2026 I wanted to set up a dependable private Minecraft server so my girlfriend and I could play together from anywhere in the world, regardless of what hardware we were on. She plays on Pocket Edition (mobile/tablet), while I play on PC Java Edition or via emulator. Achieving this meant solving two core challenges: bridging two fundamentally different multiplayer protocols (Bedrock vs. Java) and providing friction-free global connectivity without forcing non-technical players to install VPN clients or exposing my home router to open public ports. Hardware allocation: Matching workloads to the right machine I initially considered hosting everything on my always-on Intel NUC (a 6W TDP Intel Pentium N3700 running Alpine Linux). However, modern Minecraft world generation and entity ticking are heavily single-thread bound. An older, low-clocked Braswell Atom core would drop ticks and lag when players explore new areas. Instead, I designed a distributed setup across my local network: Compute Host (Windows Gaming Rig): Offloaded the actual server to my higher-performance PC featuring an 8-core / 16-thread Intel Core i7-11800H, 64-bit Eclipse Adoptium Java 25 LTS, and an NVIDIA RTX A2000 Laptop GPU. This machine easily maintains a solid 20 TPS and has the horsepower for client-side ray-traced shaders. Always-On Network Relay (Alpine NUC): Kept the low-power NUC dedicated to what it does best: 24/7 background networking, encrypted Tailscale routing, and a lightweight edge tunnel relay. PaperMC & the GeyserMC cross-platform bridge To eliminate gameplay stutter, I deployed PaperMC 26.3 instead of the default vanilla server jar for its optimized tick loop and asynchronous chunk loading. I also added the Chunky plugin to pre-render the world radius, ensuring that rapid exploration never triggers on-the-fly terrain lag. To unite mobile and PC players in the exact same world, I integrated GeyserMC : The Protocol Difference: Minecraft Java communicates over TCP port 25565 using standard Java networking. Minecraft Bedrock / Pocket Edition communicates over UDP port 19132 using the specialized RakNet gaming protocol. Standard Minecraft servers cannot talk to Bedrock clients. Real-Time Packet Translation: Geyser runs directly inside the server process, listening on UDP port 19132. It acts as an active interpreter, translating Bedrock packets into Java packets on the fly. This enables phones, tablets, and BlueStacks emulators to join alongside Java PC players seamlessly. Zero-config global connectivity with Playit.gg on Alpine While I can easily access my local servers over Tailscale , asking friends or family to install, authenticate, and configure a mesh VPN client on their phones creates friction. Traditional router port forwarding also carries security risks and requires managing dynamic DNS. To solve this, I deployed the Playit.gg tunnel daemon on my Alpine Linux NUC as a persistent background OpenRC service ( /etc/init.d/playit ) configured to start automatically on boot. Playit establishes an encrypted outbound tunnel to Anycast edge servers. When players open Pocket Edition, they simply add the generated Playit domain and port—traffic flows through the tunnel, across my internal Tailscale mesh to the gaming PC, and into Geyser with zero configuration required on their end. Troubleshooting layer 1: Bridging Playit's loopback traffic across Tailscale Deploying Playit immediately exposed a networking gap: by default, the Playit daemon assumes the game server is running on the exact same machine where the tunnel agent is installed, forwarding all incoming traffic to 127.0.0.1 (localhost). But in my architecture, the NUC is only the relay; the PaperMC server is running on my Windows gaming PC ( 100.64.20.50 over Tailscale). Because nothing on the NUC itself was listening on 127.0.0.1:19132 or 127.0.0.1:25565 , test connections timed out instantly. To bridge this gap cleanly without complicating the Playit configuration, I built a custom OpenRC background service on Alpine called minecraft-relay ( /etc/init.d/minecraft-relay ) powered by socat (a bidirectional data relay tool): Bedrock Relay: Forwards UDP packets from 127.0.0.1:19132 across the Tailscale mesh to 100.64.20.50:19132 , preserving the low-latency RakNet datagrams essential for smooth mobile gameplay. Java Relay: Forwards TCP traffic from 127.0.0.1:25565 to 100.64.20.50:25565 for standard PC Java clients. Boot Persistence: Configured OpenRC to automatically launch minecraft-relay at startup alongside Playit, ensuring that if the NUC reboots after a power outage or kernel update, the entire tunnel pipeline restores itself without manual intervention. Troubleshooting layer 2: Overcoming the Pocket Edition license paywall Once the relay was live and packet routing verified, I tested connecting from a Pocket Edition client on mobile. The server appeared online in the friends list with a green ping indicator, but clicking “Join Server” resulted in an immediate “Connection failed” error. Investigating the server console revealed the root cause: GeyserMC defaults to auth-type: online . In this mode, whenever a Bedrock player connects with their Microsoft account, Geyser contacts Mojang's authentication servers to verify if that Microsoft account also owns a paid copy of Minecraft Java Edition for PC. If the player only owns Minecraft Bedrock / Pocket Edition on Android, iOS, or a tablet, Geyser treats them as unauthorized and slams the door shut. Since we only owned Pocket Edition on our mobile devices, we needed the server to accept valid Bedrock accounts directly. I solved this by aligning authentication settings across both layers: In PaperMC's server.properties , I configured online-mode=false so the backend Java server doesn't reject bridged player UUIDs. In GeyserMC's config.yml , I switched auth-type: offline . This allows native Pocket Edition players to join directly using their Bedrock gamertags without being paywalled by a missing PC Java license. I also identified an incompatibility with Floodgate 2.2.3 , which crashed on startup due to internal class changes in Paper 26.3 ( ClassNotFoundException: net.minecraft.server.ServerConnection ). Because Geyser operates completely independently as a standalone protocol translator, removing Floodgate eliminated the crash while preserving full Bedrock cross-play functionality. The finished result: Seamless cross-play with zero client friction With both routing and authentication resolved, Pocket Edition connected immediately on the very next attempt. My girlfriend can connect seamlessly from anywhere in the world using our assigned Playit domain ( practically-nissan.tun.ply.gg:63453 ) without installing Tailscale or configuring VPN profiles on her phone. The Windows gaming rig handles world rendering, mob AI, and Chunky pre-generation with an unyielding 20 TPS, while the Alpine NUC quietly maintains the persistent network tunnel and background routing. title: BOINC & Einstein@Home Distributed Scientific Computing Node: Alpine Linux, Musl sprintf C Shim & Throttled Astrophysics Research
snippet: BOINC & Einstein@Home Distributed Scientific Computing Node: Alpine Linux, Musl sprintf C Shim & Throttled Astrophysics Research Completed Project BOINC 8.2.8 · Einstein@Home Fermi LAT · Musl sprintf C Shim · Remote GUI RPC · Completed October 17, 2026 I wante...
content: BOINC & Einstein@Home Distributed Scientific Computing Node: Alpine Linux, Musl sprintf C Shim & Throttled Astrophysics Research Completed Project BOINC 8.2.8 · Einstein@Home Fermi LAT · Musl sprintf C Shim · Remote GUI RPC · Completed October 17, 2026 I wanted to put the spare, always-on compute cycles of my home lab server to work supporting genuine astrophysics research. My Intel NUC runs Alpine Linux 24/7 as an encrypted network gateway, web server, and Tailscale relay. Rather than letting the CPU sit idle during low-traffic periods, I decided to deploy a scientific volunteer computing client to contribute compute time to open science. This project focused on contributing to Einstein@Home —a distributed computing effort searching for spinning neutron stars (pulsars) and continuous gravitational waves using observational data from NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. Workload and architecture evaluation: Why BOINC over Folding@home? Before configuring BOINC , I evaluated Folding@home (FAH) on the NUC's 6W TDP Intel Pentium N3700 processor (a 1.6 GHz quad-core Braswell Atom CPU with 4 GB of DDR3L RAM). FAH is heavily optimized for AVX/AVX2 instruction sets and modern GPUs. On a low-power, non-AVX chip without a discrete GPU, biological simulation work units take days to complete and risk missing strict 24-to-48-hour return deadlines, while pushing CPU temperatures up continuously. In contrast, the Berkeley Open Infrastructure for Network Computing ( BOINC ) ecosystem offers critical advantages for low-power edge hardware: Flexible Deadlines: Einstein@Home tasks come with generous 14-day completion windows, giving low-clocked processors ample time to finish without failing or discarding work. Granular Resource Governance: BOINC allows precise execution throttling (down to the percentage level), strict core limits, and configurable RAM boundaries, preventing background scientific calculations from interfering with production services. Strict resource governance: Tuning the client profile Because the NUC also serves my portfolio website and acts as an encrypted network router, scientific computing must never degrade system responsiveness or trigger out-of-memory kernel panics. I tuned /var/lib/boinc/global_prefs_override.xml with strict operational parameters: Single-Core Cap ( max_ncpus_pct = 25% ): Restricts BOINC to utilizing at most 1 of the NUC's 4 cores, leaving 3 full CPU cores 100% available for system services, Docker containers, and network packet switching. Execution Throttling ( cpu_usage_limit = 50% ): Enforces a 50% CPU execution throttle. The BOINC process executes for 0.5 seconds and sleeps for 0.5 seconds, preventing sustained thermal buildup and keeping the CPU core temperature hovering around an easy 58°C (136°F). Memory Boundary ( ram_max_used_busy_pct = 20% / 768 MB): Dedicated 768 MB of the NUC's 3.75 GiB usable RAM to BOINC, leaving over 3 GB reserved for host operations and preventing disk swap thrashing. Load Pause Threshold ( suspend_if_no_recent_input = 0 , suspend_cpu_usage = 50% ): Automatically suspends scientific calculations if non-BOINC system load exceeds 50%, ensuring that web requests or file transfers receive immediate priority. Engineering around Alpine Linux & Musl libc obstacles Running pre-compiled scientific research binaries on Alpine Linux presents unique challenges because scientific computing projects are almost universally built against GNU C Library ( glibc ), whereas Alpine uses the lightweight musl libc . Deploying Einstein@Home exposed three distinct compatibility hurdles that I diagnosed and resolved: 1. GNU Coreutils filesystem telemetry BOINC client scripts monitor disk capacity using GNU coreutils syntax: stat --file-system -c %a ... . On standard Alpine installations, BusyBox provides the default stat utility, which lacks the --file-system flag and caused disk space verification checks to fail silently. Installing the full GNU coreutils package resolved the argument mismatch and allowed BOINC to report disk storage accurately. 2. Headless Remote RPC Administration Because the NUC operates headlessly without a local monitor attached, managing projects through a desktop GUI required remote access. I configured the BOINC daemon to accept remote GUI RPC over port 31416 ( --allow_remote_gui_rpc ) protected by gui_rpc_auth.cfg and locked down to internal Tailscale IP interfaces. This allows full graphical management from BOINC Manager on my desktop workstations across my encrypted tailnet. In addition, I created a custom local command-line monitoring utility ( /usr/local/bin/boinc-status ) that queries the local RPC socket and formats attached projects, task progress percentages, deadlines, and memory footprints directly in the terminal. 3. The Musl sprintf overlapping buffer crash & custom C compatibility shim When Einstein@Home downloaded its binary and initialized NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) planetary ephemeris calculation for the Fermi LAT pulsar search, the process immediately aborted with a segmentation fault. Tracing the crash in gdb revealed an architectural divergence between glibc and musl: legacy scientific C code in the astronomy binary invoked sprintf(buf, "%s.%d", buf, 405) —reading from and writing to the exact same memory buffer. Under glibc, this undefined behavior happens to succeed by coincidence. Under musl libc, sprintf immediately resets or writes to the start of the destination pointer before parsing the arguments, corrupting the input string in place and causing an instant memory crash. In addition, the binary attempted to call sched_setscheduler with real-time priority parameters disallowed under Alpine's unprivileged execution model. Because the project binaries are compiled and signed by the research institution, I could not rewrite the source code directly. Instead, I developed and compiled a lightweight C compatibility shim ( /usr/local/lib/libboinc_compat.so ): Buffered sprintf interception: Intercepts sprintf calls using dlsym(RTLD_NEXT, "sprintf") , formats the output into a safe temporary scratch buffer, and copies the completed string into the destination buffer only after formatting is complete, safely handling overlapping memory. Scheduler priority stubbing: Catches sched_setscheduler calls and returns success ( 0 ) rather than permitting priority violations that fail under musl. OpenRC Integration: Configured /etc/init.d/boinc to inject the shim on startup via export LD_PRELOAD=/usr/local/lib/libboinc_compat.so . Live research results With the compatibility shim and resource governor in place, Einstein@Home launched cleanly and verified its NASA ephemeris tables. The node is actively processing Fermi Large Area Telescope gamma-ray pulsar search tasks ( LATeah2224F ) under host ID 13284543 (User: Andrew Van Ek ). With 1 core capped at 50% execution throttle, the Braswell processor runs cool and silent, dedicating spare cycles to mapping our galaxy's pulsars without compromising the performance, stability, or responsiveness of my home lab. BOINC distributed computing · Einstein@Home project · NASA Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope · Alpine Linux
