snippet: Home Network Upgrade: TP-Link Archer AX3000, Tether App Management & Multi-Switch Wired Extension Completed Project Router and modem migration; mobile app administration; multi-switch wired infrastructure · Completed October 16, 2026 To establish a faster, mor...
content: Home Network Upgrade: TP-Link Archer AX3000, Tether App Management & Multi-Switch Wired Extension Completed Project Router and modem migration; mobile app administration; multi-switch wired infrastructure · Completed October 16, 2026 To establish a faster, more dependable backbone for my home lab, servers, and daily computing devices, I overhauled my local network infrastructure. I replaced an older modem and legacy Netgear router with a new TP-Link Archer AX3000 Wi-Fi 6 router. The upgrade significantly boosted wireless bandwidth and reduced latency while adding modern app-based management through the TP-Link Tether app on my phone. Expanding wired connectivity with two unmanaged switches While Wi-Fi handles phones and laptops, my servers, desktop PCs, and lab gear need dedicated, low-latency physical connections. Because consumer routers include only four standard LAN ports, I integrated two unmanaged Gigabit Ethernet switches into the topology to expand physical port capacity across different areas of my workspace. Using unmanaged switches delivered simple, plug-and-play distribution without the management overhead or misconfiguration risks of VLAN routing, maintaining line-rate Gigabit switching between local nodes. Structured cabling: Cat5e and Cat6 deployments To connect the Archer AX3000, switches, and endpoints, I ran and terminated various types of Ethernet cabling chosen for each run's requirements: Cat6 cabling : Deployed for high-throughput trunk connections between the router and switches, as well as connections to primary workstations and servers (including my Alpine Linux Intel NUC), ensuring full Gigabit throughput with extra headroom against crosstalk. Cat5e cabling : Utilized for secondary endpoints, peripherals, and intermediate patch runs where 1 Gbps performance is maintained reliably over shorter distances. App management and network verification The TP-Link Tether app allows me to manage the Archer AX3000 directly from my phone, streamlining tasks like monitoring connected clients, adjusting Wi-Fi settings, configuring guest access, and troubleshooting without needing a browser session on a desktop computer. I verified Gigabit link negotiation across both switches, validated DHCP lease assignment, and confirmed stable, low-latency throughput across both wired and wireless devices.

snippet: Acoustic Piano Audio Visualizer: Chordal Resonance, Sunbeam Swells & Apple Silicon VideoToolbox Completed Project Full-track 1080p 30fps MP4 render; piano spectral envelope; sunbeam chord illumination · Completed October 16, 2026 After developing visualizers f...
content: Acoustic Piano Audio Visualizer: Chordal Resonance, Sunbeam Swells & Apple Silicon VideoToolbox Completed Project Full-track 1080p 30fps MP4 render; piano spectral envelope; sunbeam chord illumination · Completed October 16, 2026 After developing visualizers for high-energy EDM and mellow lo-fi beats, I tackled a third distinct acoustic profile: solo acoustic piano and ambient focus music. Using the track “Quiet Focus” (3 minutes 30 seconds / 6,300 frames), I designed a specialized Pycairo and VideoToolbox rendering pipeline tailored to the expressive harmonics of grand piano acoustics. I collaborated with Antigravity CLI and ChatGPT Codex to build the spectral analysis math, tune the chordal envelope followers, and implement the hardware-accelerated rendering script. Engineering a chordal resonance envelope Unlike electronic tracks built on heavy 808 sub-bass, spectral scanning revealed that Quiet Focus contains virtually no sub-50 Hz rumble. Its power is concentrated in fundamental piano keystrokes (70 Hz to 750 Hz) and delicate harmonic overtones (750 Hz to 2,400 Hz). To capture realistic piano acoustics, I engineered a specialized envelope follower: a fast 0.16 attack registers the crisp percussive strike of piano hammers hitting strings, while an elongated 0.90 release decay mirrors the natural acoustic sustain of the soundboard and sustain pedal ringing out through the room. This avoids the abrupt pulsing of EDM visualizers and creates a gentle, resonant swell. Visual architecture and harmonic lighting I paired the music with a 16:9 cinematic render of an elegant grand piano beside floor-to-ceiling glass windows overlooking misty pine mountains and morning golden light: Sunbeam Chord Illumination: A diagonal radial gradient positioned along the sunlight path (x=1500, y=300) dynamically expands and warms in brightness when rich chords ring out, creating the impression of sound filling the sunlit room. Floating Dust in Sunbeams: 75 atmospheric dust motes drift with natural sinusoidal motion through the light beams, swaying gently with chord strikes. Upper-Left Frosted Glass HUD: A translucent obsidian card (x=75, y=75) sits unobtrusively over the mountain sky, featuring a rotating vinyl/metronome spool, Courier typography, live elapsed/total timestamps (e.g. [01:15 / 03:30] ), and an amber focus status beacon. Silky Melodic Wave Ribbon: A smoothly interpolated waveform ribbon rendered with a golden-to-peach gradient that translates live piano octave frequencies into fluid undulations across a baseline progress dot. Hardware-accelerated pipeline The complete 6,300-frame 1080p video was rendered by piping uncompressed 32-bit ARGB frame buffers directly from Pycairo memory into FFmpeg over standard input. FFmpeg encoded the stream using Apple's h264_videotoolbox hardware encoder at 14 Mbps with 320 kbps AAC stereo audio, delivering artifact-free playback ready for QuickTime and streaming. title: Lo-Fi Beat Audio Visualizer: Organic Damping, Ambient Lamp Breathing & Hardware VideoToolbox Rendering
snippet: Lo-Fi Beat Audio Visualizer: Organic Damping, Ambient Lamp Breathing & Hardware VideoToolbox Rendering Completed Project Full-track 1080p 30fps MP4 render; STFT audio-reactive ribbon; warm ambient lamp breathing · Completed October 16, 2026 Following my earlie...
content: Lo-Fi Beat Audio Visualizer: Organic Damping, Ambient Lamp Breathing & Hardware VideoToolbox Rendering Completed Project Full-track 1080p 30fps MP4 render; STFT audio-reactive ribbon; warm ambient lamp breathing · Completed October 16, 2026 Following my earlier high-energy EDM visualizer experiments, I wanted to create a dedicated visualizer workflow tailored specifically for chillout, lo-fi hip-hop beats. While EDM demands aggressive transient snaps, radial spiky frequency bars, and electric neon contrast, lo-fi calls for an entirely different aesthetic: warmth, nostalgic texture, and slow, organic movement. With assistance from Antigravity CLI and ChatGPT Codex, I developed a Python and Pycairo rendering pipeline to produce a 1080p music video for the chill study track “Midnight Pages” (2 minutes 22 seconds / 4,286 frames). Adapting the STFT mechanics for mellow audio dynamics To capture the relaxed feel of a lo-fi track without erratic flickering or strobing, I reworked the Short-Time Fourier Transform ( STFT ) spectral analysis parameters. I used a 2,048-point Hanning window on the 44.1 kHz decoded PCM stream to isolate sub-bass and kick transients between 30 Hz and 160 Hz while mapping mid and upper musical content across 64 logarithmically spaced frequency bands from 60 Hz to 7,000 Hz. A Hanning window acts like a smooth mathematical bell-curve fade on each tiny slice of audio. Without this gradual taper, cutting audio with sharp square edges creates artificial high-frequency cliffs (spectral leakage)—fake digital static that was not in the original song. Instead of the fast 0.35s attack and 0.84s release used for dance music, I implemented an organic envelope follower with a gentle 0.20 rise and an elongated 0.92 warm release decay. An envelope follower acts like draping a smooth blanket over the raw audio waveforms so graphics track the overall volume shape rather than buzzing like a blurry electric toothbrush. The extended 0.92 decay mimics a real physical speaker cone gently settling, transforming the kick response into a slow, rhythmic “breathing” pulse that feels natural rather than jarring. Scene composition and audio-reactive layers I paired the music with a 16:9 widescreen anime-style late-night study scene: an open notebook on a wooden desk beside a rain-streaked window overlooking a midnight city skyline. The pipeline composites several reactive elements over this scene: Ambient Lamp Breathing: A multi-stop radial amber gradient centered directly on the vintage brass desk lamp bulb (x=1220, y=260) that gently expands and brightens across the desk surface in synchrony with the low-frequency envelope. Floating Atmospheric Particles: A system of 70 floating dust motes with randomized drift vectors and phases that subtly glow in response to sub-bass intensity. Upper-Left Frosted HUD Player: A translucent dark charcoal slate card positioned over the rainy window pane, keeping the notebook and desktop scenery visible. It features a spinning vinyl/cassette spool graphic rotating smoothly at constant RPM, clean Courier and Helvetica typography, live elapsed/total timestamps, and a pulsing red recording status indicator. Undulating Audio Ribbon: Inside the HUD card, an audio-reactive ribbon renders a continuous, smoothly interpolated waveform curve across a baseline with a live progress dot, filled with a warm golden-to-peach gradient reflecting real-time frequency changes. Analog Scanlines: Subtle horizontal scanlines with 3.5% opacity and a soft vignette add authentic retro CRT warmth. Pipeline efficiency and Apple Silicon encoding The complete video comprises 4,286 individual uncompressed 1080p ARGB frames. An ARGB surface provides an uncompressed 32-bit digital canvas where every pixel carries an Alpha (transparency) channel alongside Red, Green, and Blue, allowing Pycairo to render smooth anti-aliased geometry, glowing gradients, and translucent frosted-glass overlays. Streaming raw 32-bit BGRA frame buffers directly from Cairo memory into FFmpeg over standard input eliminated intermediary disk writes. FFmpeg encoded the video using Apple's hardware-accelerated h264_videotoolbox encoder at 14 Mbps with 320 kbps AAC stereo audio, rendering the entire 2.3-minute video cleanly in just over 7 minutes. title: AI-Powered NCS Circular Audio Visualizer: STFT Spectral Analysis & Apple Silicon VideoToolbox
snippet: AI-Powered NCS Circular Audio Visualizer: STFT Spectral Analysis & Apple Silicon VideoToolbox Completed Project Dual EDM visualizer videos rendered; 1080p 30fps VideoToolbox encoding; sub-bass pulse & radial FFT · Completed October 15, 2026 When working with f...
content: AI-Powered NCS Circular Audio Visualizer: STFT Spectral Analysis & Apple Silicon VideoToolbox Completed Project Dual EDM visualizer videos rendered; 1080p 30fps VideoToolbox encoding; sub-bass pulse & radial FFT · Completed October 15, 2026 When working with fresh electronic dance music tracks, standard audio players only show static cover art or basic linear waveforms. I wanted to create a genuine NoCopyrightSounds (NCS) style circular audio visualizer video matching the exact track duration: a pulsing central disc that physically thumps to the sub-bass kick transients, surrounded by radial frequency bars, floating atmospheric particle embers, subtle bass-reactive zoom pulses, and clean modern typography. With assistance from Antigravity CLI and ChatGPT Codex, I built a fully automated generation pipeline that turns any audio file into a finished 1080p MP4 ready for streaming or video editing in iMovie. Engineering the audio spectral analysis Audio visualization requires more than just raw waveforms; it requires perceived frequency response that matches human hearing. I extracted the high-fidelity 44.1 kHz PCM audio directly via an FFmpeg pipe into NumPy and SciPy. For every video frame, the pipeline computes a Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) with a 2,048-point Hanning window to prevent spectral leakage. A Hanning window is a smooth bell-shaped curve applied to each slice of audio so it smoothly fades in at the beginning and fades out at the end, eliminating sharp artificial edges that would otherwise create fake high-frequency noise in the math. To produce the classic NCS look, the analysis separates sub-bass transients from higher musical content: low-frequency energy between 25 Hz and 135 Hz (the thump of kick drums and 808 bass) drives the circle's physical radius pulse and background zoom. This pulse is smoothed with an asymmetrical envelope follower—acting like a soft blanket over the raw waveform so the graphics follow the overall volume silhouette rather than vibrating like a blurry electric toothbrush. A fast 0.35 attack gives an immediate punch on kick hits, while an 0.84 release allows natural decay, mimicking a real speaker cone settling. The audible spectrum from 40 Hz to 12 kHz is mapped across 90 logarithmically spaced frequency bins with high-frequency boosting to compensate for the natural rolloff of electronic mixes, mirrored symmetrically around the circle. Human hearing is logarithmic (octaves double in frequency with each step), so logarithmic spacing ensures balanced visual real estate across bass, midrange melodies, and treble rather than crowding 90% of the display with high-frequency cymbals. High-resolution vector rendering and AI scene generation For the visuals, I used AI image generation to craft widescreen 16:9 cinematic backdrops tailored to the music: an alpine sunrise with radiant golden, cyan, and violet light beams bursting through twilight clouds for Version 1, and a synthwave cybernetic wireframe landscape with aurora borealis for Version 2. Embedded cover art was extracted, circular-clipped, and nested inside the pulsing center badge with radial vignette depth. The visual elements were rendered using Pycairo vector graphics onto an ARGB image surface—a 32-bit digital canvas where every pixel carries an Alpha transparency channel alongside Red, Green, and Blue, enabling smooth anti-aliased geometry, glowing gradients, and translucent overlays. Each frame features 90 radial spectrum bars with anti-aliased rounded caps, a vibrant cyan-to-magenta spectral gradient, an ambient field of 70 floating particles with audio-reactive glow, and modern sans-serif typography showing track title and artist alongside a synchronized playback progress indicator. Hardware-accelerated encoding with Apple Silicon VideoToolbox Generating 5,250 individual 1080p frames can easily become a bottleneck if written to disk as intermediary image sequences. To maximize performance, the Python rendering loop streams raw 32-bit BGRA frame buffers directly into FFmpeg through standard input. FFmpeg encodes the video using Apple's h264_videotoolbox hardware encoder at a 14 Mbps bitrate while muxing the original audio stream at 320 kbps AAC. The resulting MP4 files match the source audio length down to the millisecond, play smoothly in QuickTime and iMovie, and provide an automated, high-quality audio visualizer workflow without requiring expensive commercial video editing plugins. title: Google Cloud Folding@home VM: Automatic Daily Compute & Private Linux Desktop
snippet: Google Cloud Folding@home VM: Automatic Daily Compute & Private Linux Desktop Completed Project Eight-thread folding, checkpoint resume, and private desktop verified · Completed October 15, 2026 I built a Google Compute Engine VM to contribute computing power ...
content: Google Cloud Folding@home VM: Automatic Daily Compute & Private Linux Desktop Completed Project Eight-thread folding, checkpoint resume, and private desktop verified · Completed October 15, 2026 I built a Google Compute Engine VM to contribute computing power to Folding@home while keeping its startup, remote access, and cloud credit use manageable. The finished setup runs Debian Linux with eight virtual CPUs, starts folding without a browser login, and provides an XFCE desktop through my private Tailscale network. I connected from my Mac and signed into my existing Folding@home account so the machine could sit alongside the other computers I manage. Choosing hardware within the trial's limits I started with Google's $300 free-trial credit and checked the account restrictions before choosing the VM. GPUs were unavailable on the unupgraded trial, and concurrent Compute Engine use was limited to eight cores. I chose a compute-optimized c2-standard-8 with eight vCPUs, 32 GiB of memory, and a 30 GiB persistent boot disk. The eight vCPUs represent four physical cores with two hardware threads each. The first creation attempt failed because the selected Iowa zone did not have enough capacity. The project's quota allowed the machine, but that did not guarantee hardware availability. Moving the same configuration to another zone in the region succeeded. I kept the account on the free trial instead of enabling paid billing to obtain different hardware. Making both the VM and the folding client automatic I configured a Compute Engine instance schedule to start the VM at 8 AM and stop it at 11 PM every day in America/Detroit time. The schedule follows local daylight-saving changes. Google's scheduler received a custom role containing only the permissions to start and stop this particular instance. An additional systemd timer inside Linux requests an 11 PM shutdown as a fallback. Starting the VM is only half the automation. The official Folding@home 8.5.6 client runs as an enabled systemd service, and the boot script configures all eight CPU threads and sends the client its fold command. It can resume a saved work unit or request new work when available without someone opening Firefox or pressing Fold. I corrected the initial seven-thread setting and verified that the running simulation used eight threads. I also planned for the credit balance. At the observed undiscounted rate, fifteen running hours used about $6.26 of compute credit per day, with disk, IP, and network costs additional. I configured a fixed November 23 cutoff to stop the VM and prevent the daily schedule from continuing indefinitely. That date is a time limit, not a dollar cap, and the credit is shared with any other projects using the same billing account. The account remains unupgraded. Providing a persistent desktop through Tailscale I installed a lightweight XFCE desktop on an Xvfb virtual display and used x11vnc to share that display. Separate systemd services start the display, desktop, VNC server, and Tailscale at boot. The VM has a dedicated cloud network with no public inbound VNC rule and no Google service account attached. The VNC server listens only on loopback. Tailscale Serve forwards its desktop port to devices permitted by my tailnet's access rules, keeping the desktop off the public internet. I completed Tailscale enrollment myself, then verified the VNC protocol handshake and opened the desktop in TigerVNC on my Mac. A direct Tailscale connection measured about 18–19 milliseconds during the connection check. I also signed into Folding@home privately rather than putting credentials in the setup notes. Testing persistence and recording the result I tested a clean VM stop and start, confirmed that the services returned, and checked that Folding@home resumed its saved checkpoint. The simulation log showed eight CPU threads, and the signed-in control panel displayed the new machine processing a work unit. The persistent disk keeps the client identity, checkpoints, desktop files, and browser profile across nightly shutdowns; an unsaved graphical session itself does not survive a shutdown. The completed result is a scheduled Linux research worker with automatic client startup and private graphical access. I verified active computation, checkpoint recovery, and the remote desktop connection. A full work unit had not yet finished during setup, and the future daily schedule had not yet run at its scheduled times. Cloud scheduling can also be delayed or affected by capacity availability, so those limits remain part of the documentation. Codex helped check the restrictions, provision the VM, configure services and scheduling, test the connection, and maintain a local text log of the commands and results. I selected the project and resource goal, approved the restricted scheduler and tailnet access, and completed account sign-in. The main lesson was to verify each layer separately: available quota, deployable hardware, VM scheduling, client startup, saved work, and the actual desktop connection. title: Azure Linux VM for Folding@home: Private Remote Desktop & On-Demand Compute
snippet: Azure Linux VM for Folding@home: Private Remote Desktop & On-Demand Compute Completed Setup CPU folding verified; VNC reachable through Tailscale; scheduled shutdown at 11 PM Eastern · Completed October 15, 2026 I wanted a second source of computing power for ...
content: Azure Linux VM for Folding@home: Private Remote Desktop & On-Demand Compute Completed Setup CPU folding verified; VNC reachable through Tailscale; scheduled shutdown at 11 PM Eastern · Completed October 15, 2026 I wanted a second source of computing power for Folding@home, but I also wanted to understand and control the cloud machine doing the work. The goal was a small Linux VM that I could start when I wanted to use it, reach from different networks through my private Tailscale network, and leave off when I was finished. I chose Folding@home for scientific research and kept the machine focused on that purpose. Working through Azure Student quota and regional availability The first challenge came before Linux was installed. My Azure for Students subscription did not have quota for the two-core VM family I initially selected. Asking Azure to raise that family limit did not succeed, and other VM families that appeared to have quota were unavailable in the region. A displayed quota number was not enough: the size also had to be deployable for this subscription in the selected region. I kept the deployment draft and compared the available choices instead of creating a larger or more expensive machine by accident. I also found that an availability-zone selection was restricting the size picker. After removing the zone requirement, Azure showed a supported option: a Standard B2s_v2 with two virtual CPUs and 8 GB of memory in West US 2. The disk and network resources were reviewed as part of the same deployment, and I checked the estimate before creating anything. The B2s_v2 is a burstable size, not a sustained-performance compute size. It has a baseline CPU level and a credit balance that can support activity above that baseline for a time. That makes it a reasonable small starting point, but it also sets a real limit for continuous Folding@home: if the VM spends its CPU credits, sustained work can be throttled toward the baseline. I accepted that trade-off for this experiment and limited the Folding client to one CPU thread. I will watch how it behaves rather than assume a burstable VM can run flat out indefinitely. Planning for cost and reducing exposed access Cloud compute is billed while the VM is running, so I enabled Azure's automatic shutdown for 11 PM Eastern. The intended routine is to start the machine when I want to use it and let Azure deallocate it overnight. Deallocation stops the VM compute charge, while storage and the public IP can still have a small ongoing cost. After deployment, the Overview page initially appeared inconsistent with the shutdown setting, so I refreshed the VM properties and verified the saved 11 PM schedule instead of relying only on the earlier review screen. I also treated remote desktop access as a separate security problem. Azure's network security group permits SSH only from my current client address. I did not add an inbound rule for VNC. TigerVNC is configured to listen on the VM's loopback interface, and Tailscale Serve forwards its port to the private tailnet. That gives my authorized Tailscale devices a route to the desktop without making the VNC service reachable from the public internet. I tested the connection from my Mac and received the expected VNC protocol handshake. Keeping the Linux desktop lean and making Folding@home work I installed Ubuntu Server 24.04 and added a lightweight XFCE desktop so the VM could also provide a graphical environment. My first desktop package installation began pulling in recommended extras such as printing, Bluetooth, and media applications. That was more than this small server needed, so I stopped that package pass and installed only the required components without recommendations. I then configured TigerVNC for a 1440 by 900 desktop and kept the VNC password private by entering it directly on the VM myself. Next I installed the official Folding@home Linux client and checked its service and control interface. The client downloaded a work unit and started its CPU core on one thread with no GPU assigned. That verified the full path from installation to active computation; it does not yet claim that a work unit has finished or been returned. The service starts with the VM, while the Azure shutdown schedule bounds how long the cloud machine stays allocated overnight. Fixing the desktop after the first remote login Connecting over Tailscale worked, but the minimal desktop exposed one more missing piece: clicking its globe-shaped browser icon produced an I/O error. The desktop image did not include a browser, and Ubuntu's Firefox package depends on Snap for the actual browser installation. After installing Firefox, I found that XFCE's browser launcher also called xdg-settings , which was absent because I had deliberately omitted recommended desktop packages. I installed xdg-utils and its supporting packages, then tested the XFCE browser launcher; it opened Firefox successfully. I also installed the OpenAI Codex CLI and Google's Antigravity CLI for terminal work. Both commands were missing on the initial desktop, so I installed them as my normal user, put their directory on the shell path, and checked their reported versions in a fresh terminal. The final setup has Codex CLI 0.163.0 and Antigravity's agy CLI 1.3.6. I completed the cloud and Tailscale configuration, but kept account sign-in for those coding tools in my own hands. What the finished setup proves The result is an Ubuntu VM that can contribute one CPU thread to Folding@home, provide a lightweight XFCE desktop over VNC, and accept that desktop connection only through my tailnet. I verified the VNC handshake, confirmed the Folding@home and VNC services were active, and checked that Tailscale Serve identified the forwarding as tailnet-only. I also confirmed that the public Azure network rules still had no VNC port. This project took persistence in several different forms: an unsuccessful quota request, VM sizes that were unavailable despite appearing plausible, a regional availability setting that hid a usable choice, a shutdown status that needed rechecking, an oversized package recommendation set, and a desktop shortcut that depended on an omitted utility. Each time, I checked the actual system state and changed only the part that was blocking progress. The useful outcome is not just a working VM; it is a setup whose limits, access path, and shutdown behavior I can explain and verify.
