content: Getting Useful Commands onto an Older Slax System Completed Project Updated October 15, 2026 I worked on a customized Slax Linux system where several newer command-line tools would not run because they require newer system libraries. Normal network file-transfer options were also unavailable during troubleshooting. I selected a self-contained version of BusyBox, a program that bundles dozens of core utilities into a single executable, and prepared the binary files in Debian through Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). When the Live Kit init script halted at startup because it could not find an executable chroot command in the merged filesystem union, I integrated the standalone BusyBox and 64-bit chroot binaries directly into /slax/rootcopy/ and patched lib/livekitlib inside initrfs.img with an automatic fallback. This bypassed the startup halt, restored normal boot into the persistent desktop session, and made BusyBox and standard Linux admin utilities immediately available across the environment.

content: Persistent Network Storage on My Intel NUC Completed Project I set up a USB drive on my Intel NUC as shared network storage that I can access from both Windows and Mac. The NUC runs Alpine Linux and uses Samba, software that lets Linux provide a shared drive to other computers. I worked through the drive mounting, login permissions, and automatic startup so the storage stays available without rebuilding the setup each time the NUC restarts. content: Private Local-AI Portfolio Assistant Dynamic Local Answers Updated October 15, 2026 I built the chatbot in the corner of this website to answer questions about my experience, skills, and projects. It now runs NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano 4B locally on my Windows PC through LM Studio. Visitor messages pass through my Alpine Linux Intel NUC and a private SSH connection over Tailscale. The website assistant has no cloud fallback and no tools to read files, run commands, download videos, or control devices. The project evolved from getting the model connection and startup recovery working to testing what visitors could make it say. Earlier tests showed that a system prompt alone did not reliably keep the model on topic, so I initially restricted it to selecting a prewritten portfolio answer. I replaced that answer-selection flow with dynamic generation. The gateway retrieves relevant curated portfolio notes and sends them to Nemotron with the visitor's question. The model writes a fresh answer tailored to the question, with instructions to use those notes, acknowledge missing information, and stay focused on my documented work. These are generated explanations rather than a menu of stored replies; grounding reduces unsupported claims but does not guarantee perfect factuality. The gateway retains five requests per rolling minute per visitor IP, request and answer size limits, one website inference at a time, and screening for unrelated or instruction-changing requests. Client-supplied conversation history is rejected, so each question should stand on its own. Private, rotated prompt logs use pseudonymous client identifiers and redact common credential patterns; the chat interface discloses logging. I tested distinct generated answers to portfolio questions and checked that unrelated and instruction-changing requests were refused. The separate phone assistant shares the same Windows model but has its own general-purpose prompt and spoken-response pipeline. Both request a thirty-minute idle unload timer; the gateway allows additional time for loading and generation. I will continue checking answer quality and portfolio coverage as projects change. title: Sudoku Vision & Cognitive Reasoning Engine
snippet: Sudoku Vision & Cognitive Reasoning Engine Live & Interactive Computer Vision · Heuristic Deduction · Zero-Idle Architecture · October 23, 2026 The Concept Inspired by interactive browser-based portfolio demos, I wanted to showcase an active, visible problem-s...
content: Sudoku Vision & Cognitive Reasoning Engine Live & Interactive Computer Vision · Heuristic Deduction · Zero-Idle Architecture · October 23, 2026 The Concept Inspired by interactive browser-based portfolio demos, I wanted to showcase an active, visible problem-solving task operating client-side in the browser. With assistance from Antigravity CLI, I designed and engineered an event-driven computer vision and cognitive reasoning pipeline. While game bots like Connect 4 are typically driven by canned minimax tree searches, Sudoku provides a compelling stage for true cognitive reasoning: constraint propagation, candidate elimination, pedagogical rule explanation, and search-tree backtracking. What Got Built Optical Scan & Grid Ingestion: A client-side drag-and-drop upload zone that accepts photos and screenshots of Sudoku puzzles (from morning newspapers, paperback puzzle books, or mobile screens) and renders an optical alignment grid overlay onto HTML5 Canvas. Includes four authentic pre-rendered styles (Newspaper, Modern Mobile App, Puzzle Book, and Diabolical Escargot). Interactive 9×9 Digital Verification Grid: A responsive, keyboard-navigable 9×9 board with 3×3 box demarcations, arrow-key navigation, candidate pencil marking, and manual digit override before initiating solving. Pedagogical Cognitive Engine: A human-like deduction engine that evaluates candidate numbers (1–9) per cell, prioritizes deterministic logical rules (Sole Candidates and Hidden Candidates across rows, columns, and 3×3 boxes), and falls back to Minimum Remaining Values (MRV) heuristic branching when pure deduction is exhausted. Live Cognitive Thought Stream: A dark terminal-style telemetry panel streaming Nemo’s natural-language deductions in real time, with color-coded classification tags ( SOLE CANDIDATE , HIDDEN CANDIDATE , BRANCH CHOICE , BACKTRACK ), real-time deduction/backtrack counters, remaining cell tallies, and variable execution speeds ranging from pedagogical slow-step up to Turbo. Zero-Idle Compute Architecture: Because Sudoku extraction and heuristic solving are purely event-driven, the engine operates client-side with zero continuous GPU VRAM or CPU overhead on the backend infrastructure when idle. title: Mind Reader AI: In-Browser Human Randomness & Choice Predictor
snippet: Mind Reader AI: In-Browser Human Randomness & Choice Predictor In Active Development Custom ML Architecture · ONNX Web · Shannon Entropy Telemetry · Launching Tomorrow · October 24, 2026 The Concept Humans are notoriously incapable of producing true mathematic...
content: Mind Reader AI: In-Browser Human Randomness & Choice Predictor In Active Development Custom ML Architecture · ONNX Web · Shannon Entropy Telemetry · Launching Tomorrow · October 24, 2026 The Concept Humans are notoriously incapable of producing true mathematical randomness. When asked to simulate a random sequence of coin flips (Heads vs. Tails) or rapid keystrokes, cognitive biases—such as alternation bias (over-switching between choices), clustering aversion (avoiding long streaks), and subconscious rhythmic cadences—leave distinct probabilistic fingerprints. Collaborating with Antigravity CLI , I am engineering a real-time machine learning prediction engine (“Mind Reader”) that analyzes human input patterns on the fly to predict the visitor's next choice with statistically significant advantage over 50/50 baseline chance. Architecture & Technical Specifications To ensure high throughput and zero latency without exposing backend infrastructure to compute exhaustion, the engine executes entirely within the visitor’s web browser. It combines higher-order Markov transition matrices with a compact neural sequence classifier exported directly to ONNX Web format. Component Implementation Spec Performance Metric / Target Inference Runtime ONNX Runtime Web (Wasm / SIMD edge execution) < 3.5 ms per choice (zero network hops) Model Architecture Higher-Order Markov (k=3 to 5) + Bi-LSTM / FFNN Sequence Head Target 68%–78% accuracy vs. humans (50% chance) Information Theory Real-time Shannon Entropy: H(X) = -Σ P(x) log2 P(x) Quantifies non-randomness deviation from 1.000 bit Visual Telemetry Running Loss Curve, Confusion Matrix, and Confidence Bar Dual-axis Loss vs. Rounds vector graph Server Resource Cost Zero-Idle / Client-Side WebAssembly sandbox 0 MB Server VRAM • 0% Host CPU Utilization Development is actively underway with Antigravity CLI. A dedicated interactive demonstration page with real-time prediction gameplay, running loss graphs, and interactive telemetry dials will deploy tomorrow.

title: Phone AI Gateway: PIN-Free Calls to Local Nemotron
snippet: Phone AI Gateway: PIN-Free Calls to Local Nemotron Live Prototype Hotline PIN-free telephony bridge · Twilio PSTN Gateway · NVIDIA Nemotron 4B · Rate Limited Interactive Telephone Hotline Demo 📞 +1 (912) 915-3851 Call from any phone to converse aloud with Nemo...
content: Phone AI Gateway: PIN-Free Calls to Local Nemotron Live Prototype Hotline PIN-free telephony bridge · Twilio PSTN Gateway · NVIDIA Nemotron 4B · Rate Limited Interactive Telephone Hotline Demo 📞 +1 (912) 915-3851 Call from any phone to converse aloud with Nemo powered by local Nemotron 4B • Guardrails: 5-minute session limit • 1 call per 15 min per caller ID • Deferral during active GPU training. Call Hotline → I built a separate personal project for talking to AI over a phone call. The original design used Twilio to receive calls, ask for a PIN, and offer Google Gemini in the cloud or a choice of models on a Linux HP computer. It connected phone menus, speech transcription, AI inference, and spoken responses. The current flow connects incoming calls directly to one local model: NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano 4B on my Windows PC, without asking the caller for a PIN. Twilio transcribes the caller's question, the PC generates an answer, and Twilio reads it aloud. This phone AI remains general-purpose and does not use the website chatbot's portfolio-grounded instructions. Callers finish by hanging up. I removed the spoken “Done”, “goodbye”, and “bye” exit commands, so those words are treated as ordinary speech rather than commands to terminate the call. Phone inference requests set a thirty-minute idle timer in LM Studio. When the model stops receiving requests, it unloads automatically from memory; continued phone or website use of the shared model resets the idle period. The service makes no wake attempts. If the PC or its model service is unavailable, it says, “We're sorry. The PC is offline. Please try again later. Goodbye.” and ends the call. A running model service can load the downloaded model on demand for the next request. Removing the caller PIN retains Twilio signature verification, request throttling, call-bound sessions, and the fixed local model. Signed incoming calls receive a session automatically; later requests must match that call. Unsigned callbacks and requests with missing or mismatched sessions were rejected in HTTP smoke tests. The tests also confirmed the new greeting, ordinary handling of the former exit words, the thirty-minute request setting, and the offline message. I deployed and checked the signed PIN-free flow on the running gateway, then ran a real Windows-model inference with a short test idle timer and confirmed that LM Studio unloaded the model automatically. The production phone timer is thirty minutes. These checks did not place a real phone call; an incoming-call test is still needed to verify transcription, audible replies, and the complete hang-up experience over the telephone.

title: Troubleshooting an FTK Imager Crash
snippet: Troubleshooting an FTK Imager Crash Troubleshooting Case Study Documented September 21, 2026 I investigated an FTK Imager crash that happened repeatedly when I selected a small FAT32 USB drive. Windows could browse the drive normally, and its disk check report...
content: Troubleshooting an FTK Imager Crash Troubleshooting Case Study Documented September 21, 2026 I investigated an FTK Imager crash that happened repeatedly when I selected a small FAT32 USB drive. Windows could browse the drive normally, and its disk check reported no filesystem problems. Reinstalling FTK and resetting its settings did not fix the crash. I compared another USB device and then reformatted the test drive as exFAT, another drive format. FTK worked with exFAT. That gave me a practical workaround and pointed to a compatibility issue with this particular FAT32 drive, though it did not prove the exact cause.

title: About Andrew Van Ek
snippet: Background, education, computing philosophy, hands-on homelab journey, and technology stack.
content: About Andrew Van Ek. Background, education, computing philosophy, hands-on homelab journey, and technology stack. My Goal My personal goal is to help as many people as possible with their technology needs. I am passionate about the intersection of human connection and technical efficiency. My Philosophy I love solving problems—including the ones that don’t strictly "need" to be solved. My personal slogan is: “If it isn’t broke, do fix it.” I believe in continuous improvement and optimization rather than just maintenance. Persistence & Dedication I pride myself on my persistence. Whether it's staying late at work to ensure plant orders are completed or spending hours at home troubleshooting a custom operating system on an old Google Pixel, I see my projects through to the end. I’ve even reinstalled Windows multiple times just to explore different versions and find the perfect configuration. That persistence is equally visible when working with vintage hardware: rather than abandoning slow or temperamental legacy machines, I recently engineered a self-healing batch sync to migrate ~283 GB of archives across network shares to a vintage Windows XP computer with just 256 MB of RAM. Because running an Ethernet cable across the room wasn't an option, the transfer runs entirely over a vintage 802.11g Wi-Fi link. By building automated reconnect routines and delta comparisons into the pipeline, the machine chugs along through an autonomous 2.5-to-3.5-day wireless endurance trial without losing data or requiring manual intervention. My Personal Computer Fleet I maintain a fleet of seven computers across multiple eras: a vintage Windows XP workstation (256 MB RAM) dedicated to retro computing experiments and legacy network interoperability, a Dell Inspiron that I plan to run Slax Linux on, a 2011 Intel Mac running Debian, an M1 Mac running macOS 27, an HP laptop I received for free from Fishbeck, another HP laptop I received for free from a couple of friends, and an Intel NUC running Alpine Linux. On my Windows computer, I also run four virtual machines: Windows 11, macOS 26 (Tahoe), Ubuntu, and Kali Linux. Virtual machines let me try different operating systems and setups on one physical computer. Keeping this collection useful is an ongoing project. I update software, upgrade systems, maintain their configurations, and work through problems as they come up. It gives me hands-on practice caring for a mix of older and newer hardware across Windows, macOS, and Linux. Linux & Everyday Automation I enjoy tinkering with Linux, keeping older computers useful, and finding small ways to make everyday technology easier to use. My Maintenance & Experiments page records the remote-access fixes, Windows permission troubleshooting, USB setups, and local AI experiments along the way. I also love creating email rules to keep a highly organized inbox. Working with AI, I built a Google Apps Script that moves Gmail spam threads to Trash automatically every 30 minutes. Confusion Matrix → Factory Quality Control Tally Think of an automated optical scanner inspecting smartphones on an assembly line: True Positives are real defective screens caught before shipping; True Negatives are flawless phones passed to packaging; False Positives are perfect phones flagged because of a harmless speck of dust; False Negatives are loose buttons that accidentally slipped through. 2. F1-Score → The Two-Way Athlete Like evaluating an NBA basketball player: if a player only shoots one single layup all year and makes it, their shooting accuracy is 100%, but they're useless to the team! The F1-score prevents the AI from cheating by balancing aggressive catching (Recall) with cautious accuracy (Precision). 3. Shannon Entropy → Sahara vs. Michigan Weather Forecasting tomorrow's weather in the Sahara desert has 0 surprise (0.0 bits). But predicting spring weather in Michigan has high chaos and high surprise (~1.0 bit). High entropy means the coin sequence is wild noise; low entropy means there is a clear, predictable pattern. 4. SNR → Car Radio in a Tunnel Like driving into a highway tunnel while listening to FM radio: as static creeps in, you can still hear the melody until the static drowns out the music (0 dB). This sweep proves the AI detects the pattern even through 20% static. Mathematical Foundations & Research Context 1. The 50% Theoretical Ceiling In pure probability theory, an ideal Bernoulli trial with p = 0.50 is independent and memoryless. Its Shannon information entropy is exactly H(X) = 1.0 bit . Under pure mathematical randomness, no algorithm can achieve greater than 50% long-term predictive accuracy. 2. Human Cognitive Alternation Bias Extensive psychological research demonstrates that humans are systematically poor random number generators. Subjects exhibit severe Gambler's Fallacy : after 2 or 3 identical choices, they switch outcomes with p > 0.70 . Neural networks exploit this multi-step autocorrelation to achieve 65%–72% accuracy. 3. Diaconis Physical Precession In 2007, Stanford mathematicians Persi Diaconis, Susan Holmes, and Richard Montgomery proved that natural coin tosses precess in 3D space during flight. Due to tumbling physics, flipped coins spend more time with the starting face upward, landing on the same face roughly 51%–53% of the time.

title: Privacy Policy
snippet: Local-first data privacy, cookies policy, and zero-telemetry commitment.
content: Privacy Policy. Local-first data privacy, cookies policy, and zero-telemetry commitment. Data Ethics & Transparency Privacy Policy How this website and my homelab services handle network traffic, visitor telemetry, and AI conversations. 1. Zero Raw IP Address Storage ✓ Zero Raw IP Retention In accordance with my privacy principles, zero raw IP addresses or personally identifiable coordinates are ever logged, stored in databases, or published . When you visit the site, network edge requests pass through Cloudflare proxy nodes to protect my self-hosted homelab. The homepage displays coarse regional telemetry (such as approximate country, region, or city) purely to show aggregate global visitor trends. This data is derived dynamically on the edge without capturing or retaining your physical street address or exact location. 2. Local AI & Data Sovereignty (Nemo) My on-premise AI assistant ( Nemo ) runs locally on a dedicated NVIDIA RTX GPU host connected via a private Tailscale mesh network through an Alpine Linux Intel NUC gateway: No Third-Party Brokers: Prompts sent to Nemo are processed on my own private hardware. They are never sent to commercial data aggregators, advertising brokers, or public model training pipelines. Temporary Abuse Review: Transient rate-limiting checks (5 messages/minute) are enforced in memory to protect local hardware from automated denial-of-service loops. No Account Tracking: You do not need to sign in or provide an email to chat with Nemo. 3. Dual-Brain Cloud Assistant (Google Cloud Run) The companion assistant at AI Assistant runs on Google Cloud Run utilizing Vertex AI Agent Builder. Queries are strictly used to search my grounded knowledge repositories (649 GVSU IT service-desk articles and ~977 OneDrive CIS class documents). Zero personal search profiles are constructed from your inquiries. 4. Client-Side Browser Persistence (localStorage) To provide responsive interactive tools without server-side tracking, certain preferences and benchmarks are stored exclusively inside your own browser using standard localStorage : Page Load Speed Tachometer: Your fastest page render record (milliseconds) and personal visit counter stay strictly in your browser. Nemo Chat History: Your active conversation is retained on your device so you can navigate across portfolio pages without losing answers. You can clear this anytime by clicking the Clear button in the chat header. Weather Units: Temperature scale preferences (°F vs. °C) are remembered locally. None of this local data is ever transmitted back to an external tracking database. 5. Zero Third-Party Advertising Trackers This website contains zero marketing cookies, zero Facebook Pixels, and zero commercial tracking beacons . I do not run banner advertisements or monetize visitor data in any way. 6. Contact Information If you have any questions about this policy or would like to discuss homelab security and privacy practices, feel free to reach out directly via the Contact page or email avanek737383@gmail.com .
